utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could please everybody -- can we start with the appearances and then we will proceed with the hearing today. Mr. Mundis, we calculated the time and we came up with the figure of 176 minutes, which means that you have another hour. You have up until 10.05. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Did you want the appearances for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That won't be necessary because I see that we have the same faces in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday we ended in the evening, we were discussing the Ljubuski camp. I would ask now, Mr. President, with the assistance of e-court that the witness be shown what's been marked as P 9019. Mr. Vulliamy, do you see some images in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise what you see on the screen? Let me -- just a moment, let me get to the right --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I apologise for that, sir. Let me get to the right page. We are looking for the last four digits on the ERN number 2976, which I believe is about page 5. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, it's Dretelj, not Ljubuski, as Daryl Mundis had indicated. I believe he misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see an image now in front of you, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; the two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise what you see in those photographs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise it. Twice I have seen these photographs before, and the thing that makes me identify this immediately as Dretelj is in the top left-hand corner you can see the two hangars going into the sort of mound in the hillside, which makes it to me easily recognisable as Dretelj. I also recognise the shed in the middle of the picture as being the one we went into where the bags were hanging from the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of the registrar we could take the top photo full screen. Now, sir, you indicated that you recognised the tunnel. Perhaps with the assistance of the usher if we could use the smart board, I would ask that you -- the usher will assist you -- if you could please mark what you were referring to as the tunnel. And I believe we will be using red for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon me, what am I marking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could mark what you currently -- or previously indicated as the tunnel or tunnels.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here they are. There is one here, and the other one is actually behind these trees, the entrance about there, so sort of here, and this is an open space in between them. The doors would be there and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if you could, please, for the record, if you could perhaps mark that -- those lines that you've indicated with T for "tunnel." Now, sir, you've also indicated one of the hangars that you spoke about yesterday. Can you please mark that, or circle that building.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one I referred to as being the one with the plastic bags hanging, with the men on the ground. That's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you please place an H next to that, for "hanger."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if you could, please, in the bottom right-hand corner place today's date, which is the 9th of May 2006.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And please initial that or place your name on the document.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that that be captured and given an In Court identification number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit will be tendered as IC 00003, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, yesterday -- this is captured on page 100 of the transcript, at lines 14 and 15 -- you indicated, "... we came back down the gentle slope from the tunnels, there was a mealtime going on ... where some grass is on a corner." Again, this is page 100, lines 14 and 15. In this photograph, do you see this area where this mealtime was going on, where some grass is on a corner?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- I think it's about here. I don't know if everyone can see where I'm pointing. As you come down from the tunnels, it's just on the left. There is this junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be easier if we could go now to one of the other photographs. It might be more visible on one of the other photographs.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can attempt to mark it here, if the Bench would like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think we need to go, for technical reasons, actually, to another photograph or a clean version of this one. My apologies for that. Okay. Now, if you see that area where you observed the mealtime?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is it easier to see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of the usher, if you could mark the area.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's within this area here, with a cooking facility somewhere and, as I recall, the men were crouching in -- within the area of that circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask again, for the record, that you place an E inside the circle, E for "eating."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, if you could please date and initial the bottom of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We would again ask, Mr. President, that this image be captured and that it be given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit will be tendered and admitted under the reference IC 00004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask, with the assistance of the Registry, that the witness be shown a bundle of photographs via e-court that's marked as 9104. And the first image I would like to be shown to the witness is photograph number 16, which is ERN 01145482-16. Looking for number 16, the last two digits being numbers 16. Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise the image that's in front of you at --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what that is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will be one of the two tunnels. I think probably the one on the right as we looked at the photograph before. When I saw it, the door was open, but that is one of the two tunnels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could you please again date and place your initials on the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President I ask that that be give an In Court identification or an In Court exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This exhibit will be tendered and admitted under the reference IC 00005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please within the same marked Prosecution number go to the photograph bearing number 01145483, number 16. Again, the number I'm looking for is 01145483-16. Perhaps, Mr. President, for the sake of expediency, I could show the witness a hard copy of this photograph, which we do have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that that would be more practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sorry to make the usher run about, but if we can give the witness a red marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vulliamy, do you see now a photograph on the ELMO next to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what you can observe in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two buildings running along one of two pathways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise either or both of those buildings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise them specifically, but I know where they are, and I -- I know that I've walked past them but I don't recognise them from this particular view necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd ask, again with the assistance -- I'll have that photograph retrieved, please, and I have another photograph to show the witness. This one comes from the same bundle, bearing ERN number 01145483, number 11. Do you recognise the buildings in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the path, moving from left to right, along which you come from the entrance to Dretelj towards the sheds that -- the shed I marked on the first photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- end of which is on the far right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there, sir, because again we need to mark this photograph. When you say, "This is the path, moving from left to right, along which you come from the entrance to Dretelj towards the sheds," could you please mark that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The entrance is over there, and the walk towards the sheds is along the line of that arrow, and there are buildings here into which we also went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the buildings that are visible in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the one on the far right. This one for sure. That's the shed which I'm referring to as the one with the plastic bags hanging for convenience. And somewhere along here, although I'm not going to be certain as to which one it is, will be what I called the medical facility, and I think, but I can't be absolutely certain, it's that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask, sir, first of all if you could indicate by marking with a letter S the shed that you referred to, the one with the hanging plastic bags.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us that you were unsure which of the buildings were the medical facility. Can you mark the building or buildings that you believed were the medical facility.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason I'm unsure is I'm not sure which one it is. All I know is that it was on the left before you got to the shed, so it will be either that one or that one, and I think it's that one but I wouldn't want to be certain as to that. I -- the -- we had a different view of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask you, sir, if you could mark inside the circles that you placed on these two buildings M1 for the building that you think was the medical facility, and M2 for the other building which might have been the medical facility.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again with the assistance -- I'll have that photograph returned. I have one more photograph. Please, sorry, if you could have the witness date and sign that photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I have one last photograph I'd like to show the witness. This one from the same bundle, P 9107, bearing ERN number 01145483-25. Sir, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that building is, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the shed I referred to in which the women were kept on the first visit and the men crouched on the ground with the plastic bags on the second visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please again on this building, somewhere on the building, mark with an S for "shed."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And please, again, initial or sign and date this photograph.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to assign a number to this exhibit. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 01045483-11 is tendered and admitted under reference IC 00006. The second document, bearing ERN number 01 -- sorry: 01145483-25 will be tendered and admitted under the reference IC 00007. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, before moving to our next subject, I'd just like you to explain or tell the Trial Chamber approximately what time you left Dretelj on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would have been about mid- -- mid- to late afternoon, still during daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- tell the Trial Chamber where you went and what if anything happened as you were departing Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite shaken, because it had been a distressing afternoon, we drove towards Medjugorje and a car drove at us from some speed from behind and sideswiped my car. It wasn't a hard knock, hard enough to knock me off the road, but it was a -- "collision" is too strong a word. It was what we call a sideswipe, and the car then sped off ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what reporting activities you undertook the following day.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it was the following day; if not, the day after that. We were endeavouring now to get into East Mostar but we -- at the hotel in Medjugorje, word went round that there was to be a press conference on the camps and on Dretelj by authorities from Herceg-Bosna, and that would be held in Medjugorje, so we stayed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the approximate date that this press conference took place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8th -- 7th or 8th of September, something like that. 8th of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again the year?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or 9th, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall or can you remember who it was that spoke at this press conference?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only remember two names, and it was certainly a bit strange that some -- that these authorities were suddenly coming to us. I think it was laid on in Medjugorje for the benefit of the press because that's where they were based. The names were Kresimir Zubak, who, as I recall, chaired the meeting or spoke first, and the other one was Mr. Pusic. I think his first name was Branislav.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you recall what was discussed at this press conference?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What was discussed was the camp that we had been into in Dretelj the previous day specifically. More generally, the other two camps, at Gabela and Rodoc. And most of the conversation was about that. And the speakers also wanted to draw attention to camps in which Croatians were being held, Bosnian Croats were being held, by the government side, and I don't recall whether they talked about camps on the Serbian side or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Vulliamy, any of the discussions concerning Dretelj or what you were told about Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And there were slightly conflicting views coming from this panel because Mr. Zubak conceded that there had been breaches of international standards in Dretelj [Microphone not activated] and excused this, or at least he explained it by the -- by reference to the speed with which the inmates had had to be interned and he implied that this was for security reasons, and blamed it in a way that I was fairly used to by now on the actions of irresponsible individuals rather than matter of policy. The breaches, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Vulliamy, what do you mean by "in a way that I was fairly used to by now"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one had had many conversations since the war in Croatia with leadership blaming apparent atrocities on rogue elements or irresponsible individuals. It was the way in which Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serbs talked about the atrocities in Omarska and Trnopolje. It was the way in which the Serbs would talk about atrocities in Vukovar. It was a language I'd become fairly used to, that when these things were happening they would blame it on a rogue element.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time of this press conference in September, 1993, Mr. Vulliamy, did you know who Mr. Zubak was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd heard his name, and as I recall he was introduced as the vice-president or the deputy president of the HVO, but I wasn't sure what that meant. I've followed his name since, yes, in politics but at the time I wasn't sure exactly who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, at that point in time, in September, 1993, did you know who the other person that you've identified as Mr. Pusic was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He introduced himself. I hadn't heard of him but he introduced himself or was introduced as the person in charge of prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember anything that Mr. Pusic said at this press conference?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He -- he implicitly disputed what Mr. Zubak had said. He implied or said outright -- I think he did say outright that the conditions in Dretelj did meet international standards and were within the Geneva Conventions, and made a remark that I made a note of and remember, that if the tunnels were good enough for the JNA soldiers - that's the former Yugoslav army soldiers - it was good enough for the Muslim prisoners. And I thought that remark was inappropriate given what we had seen and were still fairly shocked by the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've also mentioned in this context that Gabela and Rodoc were discussed at this press conference. Did you on any occasion visit either of those two locations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, then, to where you went after this press conference and what events you reported on.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: East Mostar, which was, in a way, the -- the -- the aim was to get into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, did you in fact obtain access to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did. And I think that was the next day, which would be September 9th or 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about how it was that you were able to gain access to East Mostar on that day.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Spanish UN forces had actually abandoned their base in the city, in the east side of the city, way back in May, but they were running daily patrols or every other day patrols into the city in APC armoured vehicles which were taking passengers, and I think they were escorting aid as well, but if you arranged it, you could get a ride with them into the enclave, and that's how I got in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there other reporters that went in with you at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went with one colleague, and I don't recall how many others there were in the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what you observed when you entered East Mostar on or about 9 or 10 September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extensive damage immediately visible to the south, as you came into the -- into the pocket and crossed the lines. And the no man's land, which I recall was some sort of air facility. Through a place called Blagaj, which I had heard about, and there were signs of a few people in these gutted out houses but we drove past them into the main bit at the east of the city and we just got out of the APC. The destruction was bad, and the shooting was regular. Shelling was regular. And within about an hour, I was as frightened as I'd ever been at any stage in this war or any other. It was a terrifying place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you please describe the living conditions that you observed to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is over the course of this day and the next one. People were for the most part or as much as they could living in cellars underground. Where they were above ground, which most were by necessity, they were cowering in the flats or houses where they lived or were staying. East Mostar was basically one main street with side streets going down towards the river where there was a sight line over to the west side. And people would have to run across these cross streets as the sniper fire - crack, crack, crack - was aimed at them. Some of this main street was so dangerous that they constructed a sort of main street or a bit of it as it were a bypass through houses on the east side of the main street, that is away from the river, and they -- the -- there was a sort of road running through people's houses, and it was -- I mean, it sounds amusing, and it's not, but people had sort of set up little businesses along this main street through houses. So that if there was somebody in the house who was a hairdresser, you could get your hair cut, which I did, actually, and -- but throughout the -- the -- you could hear shooting and you could hear shelling. More regularly than any place I'd been since Vukovar, actually, certainly more regularly than in other places, like Sarajevo. It was pretty continuous. People were visibly -- visibly on edge, nervous, and rightly -- rightly frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I just would like you, if you could, perhaps clarify or expand upon this notion of what you have told us at line 25 of page 14, where you say "this main street through houses." Could you explain that in a little bit more detail?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't explain properly before. Part of this main street was so exposed to the western side that it was too -- deemed too dangerous to walk down, and too many people had been killed, either by sniper fire or mortar fire, and so they built -- they sort of -- you left the main street to go along a sort of route, a pedestrian route, behind the houses on the east side of the main street so that the sort of passageway, if you like, for pedestrians to avoid the bit of the main street that was too dangerous, cut through houses, or in some cases the remains of houses, so that -- which were sort of connected up through gardens or destroyed walls, so that you sort of walked through people's properties to avoid the risk of walking down the street, so that the "street" was actually a sort of walkway they had arranged through people's houses so as to avoid exposure to the -- the fusillade coming from the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, approximately how many people were in East Mostar at this point in time, September, 1993, when you were in that part of the city?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was told that the figure initially, when the pocket was sealed off sometime around the end of May, or June, had been 10.000 but that the numbers had now swelled to about 55.000. And what was so shocking about it and distressing was that the vast majority of those were women and children. So one was able to put together the pattern, really, that had begun back in Capljina that day. In effect, the men had gone to the camps and the women and the children had been herded through this Blagaj place into the east part of Mostar, with elderly people as well, where they were being subjected to this barrage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What places, if any, did you visit during the time that you were in East Mostar in September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visited the headquarters of the Bosnian army, or what there was of it, and visited the -- it's almost a euphemistic word, but the hospital, the attempt at a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what you observed in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was horrendous. There were people at the ground level, waiting for news or trying to get to see people who -- relatives or family who were wounded down there. Most of the attempt at medical treatment was underground, and very, very basic and very distressing. I remember in particular a girl aged, I think about 11, whose -- half of whose head had been very badly injured. I think one of her limbs had been amputated. By then anaesthetic had arrived but the doctor we spoke to - we spoke to him for a long time - had told us that previously there had been amputations without anaesthetic. He gave a figure of 400 people who'd died in his hospital alone, never mind those on the streets. I don't know if that's accurate or not; that's what he said. Most importantly for the purposes of, I thought at the time, reporting this, the hospital itself had taken several direct hits of artillery and tank fire, despite a red cross being clearly visible on it. He said that one of the -- that there had been considerable damage to the roof of the hospital, and as a result of that, his supply of medicines had been -- had been, if not destroyed, impaired. Don't know why he kept medicine in the roof. Didn't seem perhaps a good idea, but when people would try to go and repair the roof, they were being shot at by snipers. And the -- I suppose the most sort of distressing bit of all was when he offered to show us his makeshift morgue, and I said yes, all right, and went into this morgue, but it wasn't really a morgue. There was no refrigeration, there were no body bags, merely corpses, about ten or a dozen when we went in. It was a terrible place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you remember the name of this hospital, or did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name. I think it had been a hospital but it was an old Habsburg building. I can remember that. I may have written the name, I can't recall it now, I'm afraid. The doctor's name was Dragan Milavic or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, on this occasion, how long did you remain in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you on any subsequent occasion return to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late in -- mid- to late February, the following year, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what events you covered between September, 1993, and February or mid- to late February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, I was getting the book out and I -- I was covering other events in my -- in my posting. As I recall, I don't think I went to Bosnia between September, 1993, and February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, sir, about your return to Bosnia in February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- it was for the paper. And well, it started off, actually, at the Zagreb airport, flying down to Split, and in the departure lounge was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you on that occasion speak to Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did briefly. I was with a colleague from the Washington Post and we were very anxious to talk to him. Not least because we had been following events in Mostar, or at least I had, obviously, in the press, closely and with interest and despair. The -- I hadn't seen him, of course, since that night when he announced his new presidency of the HDZ, despite subsequent attempts. And I think he recognised me -- and he was cordial and I asked him immediately about Mostar. There was a plan around at the time that I'd been reading, I think -- I think the EU were talking about -- the European Union were talking about dividing the city and I think I asked him about that, and what I remember him saying was, "Mostar will remain one city. It is the capital of Herceg-Bosna." That was all I remember from the conversation. He wasn't anxious to talk, and we boarded into our separate seats and he -- we took -- declined to have a conversation at the other end when we got to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And following your arrival in Split, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Medjugorje, to try to get back into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us briefly the steps that you took at that time to get back into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By then the UNHCR had organised a sort of armoured -- I mean armoured, not armed -- convoys of aid into the east of the city, under the auspices of a remarkable man called Jerry Hume. It was a sort of -- it was a UNHCR operation but it was a rather heroic one-man operation and that was running out of Medjugorje, and again he was taking passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you on this occasion return to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, to the best of your recollection, can you give us a date or an approximate date - month and year - that were you in East Mostar on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be about the 20th or the 21st of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you observed on this occasion when you were in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, people cowering in cellars, including myself. It was very frightening to be out. The people -- there was an area of flats to the north of the pocket which were pockmarked and shelled and badly damaged, and they called it Beirut, as I recall. A lot of people had come into the centre of the pocket from this so-called Beirut, which I think was at most times of the day cut off from the -- as it were, the downtown area, if that's the right word. So people were in cellars most of the time, but there wasn't enough room. A lot of new arrivals, because the population had swelled more - I don't know by how much; again, mostly women, children and elderly - were into -- they were crowded into a theatre or a cinema or some above-ground location. They were sitting on the stairs, they were hunkered down on the floor. The sniping and the shelling, well, it wasn't continuous but it was as heavy as anything I knew. There was a doctor who I met again for the second time who I had met before who had come down from Sarajevo, and actually it wasn't just I who was making this kind of relative contrast or comparison. He said that compared to Sarajevo, this place was a nightmare. And so we interviewed more of these refugees, deportees, whatever you want to call them, and I also learned, which I hadn't known before, that the government or Muslim side held a sort of promontory of two blocks of territory over on the other side, that's to say the west side, of the river, which amazed me. I should say now that the famous bridge which had been there during my previous visit in September had by now been destroyed, and there was a sort of makeshift -- I have no idea how they built it, there was a makeshift sort of metal -- not strictly a pontoon but there was a bridge, a makeshift bridge across the river, across which you could run to the other side, where I visited very, very briefly indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you see when you visited this brief visit on to the other side, the west side?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the territory they -- or the bit of the west side that they held was, as I say, no more than two or maybe one block, but I think two, and the houses there were -- were so badly damaged they were for the most part propped up, I mean with sandbags. I mean, the walls were as much sandbag as they were masonry. We ran across the bridge, which sort of bounced and it was quite frightening, there was shooting, we got into this -- this sort of wreckage of houses. I saw smoke coming up through a sort of chimney thing from what was apparently a subterranean area, and I said Who is there, who is there? Are people living here? And the guide said yes, they are, and I wanted to go and talk to them, and stopped and he said no, you don't. See what you have to see and let's get out of here. And I did get to see the front line where soldiers who looked sort of vacant eyed, really, were holding a front line against a Bosnian Croat front line, which is a very, very short distance away across a street and a small piece of parkland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain at this front line location?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back across this makeshift bridge, as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Back into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into East Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in East Mostar on this occasion in February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No more than a couple of days. Because we were -- we were back in the cellars again, and the shelling and the shooting was as hard as ever, but word was going around, and the Bosnian army were talking about it. Someone must have had a ham radio or something that -- that there was going to be a -- that -- that the deal which -- and I'd been aware of this before, that an American called Charles Redman had been trying to negotiate, was in the offing and -- and that it was about to -- to be signed imminently and to be agreed imminently. People were talking about it. Everyone was talking about it. People were very sceptical that it was, A, true or, B, possible -- likely to hold. But I'd been aware of this before I went in, and this news came quite suddenly, on I think the second day I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'll ask you some follow-up questions concerning this matter in just a moment, but before I do, let me ask you, sir, other than the sniping and shelling, were there any sounds that you recall from the time you were in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not this visit, actually, but from the first visit, yes. There was -- one of the things they had done was to put up speakers or some sort of amplification on the other side of the river, and there would be a sort of broadcast of heavy rock metal music and patriotic songs across to the east side of the river, which people found particularly irksome, as they were intended to do, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, when you say "they had put up speakers," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, on the Bosnian Croat western side of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, beyond the destruction of the bridge that you told us about, what other changes, if any, did you notice in East Mostar between the September, 1993, visit and the February, 1994, visit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further physical destruction. I mean almost to the point of rubble in some places, especially on that western promontory, more crowding, and, well, a sort of sense of siege, siege madness, really. Mostar pocket was very small. One did hold conversations with people, but there was a sort of -- there was a sense that people were -- were -- were going to the edge of madness by now in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you tell us about leaving East Mostar in February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Over one night, the shooting and the shelling -- well, it started to die down and then it stopped and there was a morning up fairly early, shortly after first light, and it had pretty -- it had pretty much stopped and people started to come out on to the streets. There was a very strange, very strange atmosphere of sort of disbelief, and people started to emerge from their buildings or cellars on to the street. I was with a colleague called Tom Rhodes at the time and we agreed that this, we couldn't cover the story of this potential peace agreement or cease-fire, so we made arrangements to leave as soon as possible and went round to the other side of Mostar -- to the west side, I think via Medjugorje, to get a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date that you left East Mostar and went to Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the 24th of February, or the day after the 24th. I think this is the 24th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4. I'm sorry, 1994; 24 February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Vulliamy, what did you report on at this point in time in the end of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the next -- the next stage was to go to -- I mean, we heard in Medjugorje, or wherever we picked up the car - I think it was Medjugorje - that there had been a deal in Washington. That the so-called Redman Plan had been agreed to by the Bosnian Croats and the armija forces, and we went up to West Mostar to speak to the HVO, basically, about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you about that in just a moment but can you tell us first if you noticed any differences between West Mostar and East Mostar at this time.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Immediately, and -- it's almost grotesque. West Mostar there were cars driving around, there were cafes open for business, there were soldiers chatting to each other and to the girls in the cafes. I mean, it wasn't normal life because there was a siege going on, and it was militarised and I dare say they had taken some fire themselves, but it felt like normal life after East Mostar, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, sir, in the few moments we have left, you told us at lines 9 and 10 on page 24, "We went to West Mostar to speak to the HVO, basically, about this." Do you recall your discussion with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were referred by the HVO to a special sort of press operation which they had set up, and our meeting -- I don't think it was actually at their headquarters, their command headquarters, it was some other building they had set up especially to receive journalists or other kind of visitors, and we spoke to a man whose name was, I think it was Vegar, Veso Vegar, who called himself the public affairs officer or spokesman for the HVO. Whether or not that meant the whole HVO or just for Mostar, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What if anything do you recall this Mr. Vegar telling you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should stress, by the way, that there was relative quiet. The -- the, as it were, the overnight and/or during the early hours cessation of the firing and the shooting had continued into the day. There was almost nothing to be heard. And the first question to him, obviously, was what's happened and is this going to hold? I think by then we knew what had happened because we had picked up the news of what I now know to be called the Washington Agreement. But the question to him was: Is this going to hold? Is it true? And he was very emphatic that it would. I have to say I was sceptical but he was very emphatic. He said -- he said, this is -- this is -- this has been agreed. And he talked about that the -- his army were going to remobilise from this area, and he used a word which I noted and thought was very interesting, he talked about a recommencement of hostilities with the Serbs, implying that there had been a sort of cessation of hostility with the Serbs. He said we are mobilising for a recommencement of hostilities with the Serbs. Again, I was skill sceptical, and as I recall, it was his idea although it should have been mine: Did we want to go and see some of the besieging positions, the mortar positions on his side? And I -- well, Tom Rhodes and I readily agreed that we would like to, and he didn't come himself but he sent someone in our car to take us to where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go on that occasion at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to some not high ground but higher ground, above west -- above the west of the city, to a mortar position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you observe from this position?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, surreally, you observed East Mostar across the river, so it was pretty extraordinary to think what that place looked like and felt like and to think that we had been there only that morning or, more extraordinarily, yesterday, which had been so frightening. That the -- that -- well, and one observed very quickly that the mortars were not firing. Indeed, they were covered with leather caps. Whether this is something that they were all like that or this is something that Mr. Vegar just wanted us to see, I don't know, but they were, they were out of action. And clearly out of action. I mean they had stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, in the couple of minutes that are remaining, let me ask you this: You told us yesterday that you initially went down into Herzegovina in August of 1992. Can you describe for us the changes that you observed between August of 1992 and February, 1994, in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, the place had been completely transformed and, with hindsight, embittered by a war that hadn't existed in 1992, was hastily put into action during the fall of 1992, and which very suddenly ended in February, 1994. The destruction was greater; it felt like a completely different place. It had been through -- it had been into and come out of the other side of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean, sir, when you said it had been completely transformed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm thinking of Mostar most of all, when you say Herzegovina. I mean, some -- some of the places in Herzegovina were relatively unaffected; Livno, Tomislavgrad, other places I've mentioned. But with regard to the places where there had been ethnic cleansing, camps, fighting, and you asked about Herzegovina, not the same places - there were places like this in Central Bosnia too - they had been transformed because an alliance had been ruptured. I didn't know in February, 1994, whether it was intended to put it back together again or whether that would be possible in that area, but it had been transformed inasmuch as people who had been in August, 1992, I thought fighting a common enemy had now been themselves through a bloody conflict, I say war. I mean, to me, herding women and children into a pocket and shelling them isn't war, it's something worse than war, but that's another discourse. It had been through this awful experience as had I. I was -- by now -- it was my paper, actually, demanded that I leave at this point, such was the state I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President. We would ask that a few of the documents and drawings that the witness were shown be admitted, including 1784, P 8761, P 8762, and P 9497.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you ask that Exhibit 1784, which is a videotape, be admitted, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But we saw only several seconds' worth of that videotape, and how long is it in total?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The videotape, Mr. President, I believe the video -- we can check this at the next break, but I believe that the video that was marked P 1784 was simply the approximately 55-second segment that was shown to this witness. In other words, that was a cut from a longer video, so what 1784 is is the entire 55-second segment that was shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, Mr. Registrar, please assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... those four exhibits will be then admitted under the references P 1784, P 9497, P 8761, and P 8762. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we are going to start with cross-examination. Yesterday I said that Ms. Nozica or Mr. Murphy will start cross-examination and they will have 40 minutes. From now until our break we have another 25 minutes for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether it would be convenient to take the break rather early so that the Defence counsel may confer briefly about the length of cross-examination to be taken by each one? There are also, Your Honour, a few documents that I would like to check that are being copied now that may be used in cross-examination. So I wonder if that would be a convenient course for the Court to take?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We will have our break now and continue at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We are continuing with our hearing. We will work until noon and then we will have a break of hour and a half so that everybody can rest and prepare for work in the afternoon. We will work until 5 p.m. We hope that we will conclude with this witness's testimony today. Mr. Murphy, have you reached an agreement as to the allocation of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there should be no immediate problem with this witness and I think we can certainly proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: May I introduce myself. My name is Peter Murphy, I'm one of the counsel representing Bruno Stojic. Mr. Vulliamy, you have been a working journalist, I think, since about 1977; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And during the time when you were reporting from Bosnia, you were working for the Guardian newspaper in London?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Principally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Principally. The -- I'd like to ask you a little bit about your background, if I may. You attended university, I take it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you have a background in Balkan studies as part of your degree?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You mentioned that your initial interest, I think, was in Northern Ireland; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a student and then as a journalist in the television, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you -- have you ever served in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Several members of my family have at quite a senior level, but not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So your own knowledge of military affairs is really what you've picked up as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and from relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And also, so far as the Balkan affairs are concerned, one can say that your knowledge of that subject also is derived from your work as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a layman's knowledge previous to that, as a student of history, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you speak or read the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I picked up a bit as I went along. I could get by but I couldn't hold a conversation on the level of an interview and I certainly couldn't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Rather as I speak Dutch, I assume you could ask for a coffee and say good morning to people and so on.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little -- now, yes. I could probably get further than that 12 or so years ago, but not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as a journalist, when you were in Bosnia, clearly you were there at the expense of the Guardian.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you were -- your function there was to send back reports to the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: For publication the following day.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, or whenever, yes. I mean, usually the following day, it wasn't always easy to get to phones. Often it would be late or too late, but in general that as the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In fact, you referred in your testimony to difficulty of obtaining a land line for the purpose of phoning back to England.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; you had to go down to Croatia to do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. You would have to go to Split or some other place.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, there was a place called Imotski which was popular because it was the nearest telephone to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I take it that even if the article was not published the following day, it had to be newsworthy in the sense that it would have to be published within a day or two in order to be up-to-date.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the kind of article it was. I mean, that's the judgement of my editors, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And so you would be -- your job really was to go and investigate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigate, witness, do the best one could in conditions which are, as I'm sure you realise, were not easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Of course. And you would have to do that quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have to -- I didn't have to sort of dash up and down like some of the people who would work for, say, the agencies, necessarily, but you wouldn't sort of hang about, no, nor did I want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about the time that you actually spent in Bosnia and Herzegovina. During your testimony yesterday and today, you discussed events between, I suppose, August of 1992 and February of 1994. But in fact, during that period, you were really only in Bosnia and Herzegovina for certain limited periods of time.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, differing -- I mean, we were on a rotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were usually two of us within the country, and I was there sometimes for a matter of days, occasionally for a matter of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'd like to try and pin that down a little more, if I could. You gave evidence about some events that occurred in mid-August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Including a visit to what you later learned was the Dretelj camp.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And do you recall at that time in August, how long you spent in the country altogether?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the same visit in the country that began with me going to Belgrade prior to the -- yes, to going to Omarska and Trnopolje. I think that's how that same visit started, so I would have been in former Yugoslavia since late July and I don't recall but I -- I don't recall exactly how long, but it's the same visit so it would be -- yeah -- yes, then I went to Zagreb. I think that was -- I can't calculate exactly how long but it was the same visit and it was a reasonably long one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let me be a little more specific, then: During that particular time period, how long did you spend in HVO territory, if I can use that expression?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A matter of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Matter of days.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And then you were gone during September. By "gone," I mean you weren't in HVO territory during September.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I was. Yes. I was. I went to -- I went to Central Bosnia in September, and I must have been in Tomislavgrad at some point during September, if I recall. I didn't go to Mostar in September. I think I went to Vitez during September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I was just looking at -- you recall you were referred yesterday to a witness statement that you gave in 1997. Would it help if you could see that document, with the aid of the registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: This would be page 5 of the witness statement. I believe that is a Prosecution document, is it not, Mr. Registrar? The page -- yes. The 00484823. I gave you the number for page 5. Do you need the number for the first page? I'm told that 200007. 2D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the solution could be if we put that page on the ELMO. That would be a simpler solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes practice and theory are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I don't know whether everybody can see that. Can we -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: What I'm showing you, Mr. Vulliamy, is the fifth page of the witness statement that I was referring to. If you look at the first paragraph right at the top there, it refers to covering ethnic cleansing of Muslims by the Serbs in north-western Bosnia until September, and you say, "Then I took some time off and returned to Herzegovina in mid- to late October." Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The first sentence refers to following up on the convoys like the one that I went on from north-western Bosnia into Travnik, and I think I went up to Travnik to write an article about how they were continuing, or to research an article about how they were continuing. And when I say "time off," I don't mean holiday. I was working elsewhere, and yes, that makes sense. I returned in October to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I don't mean to press it unnecessarily. I just -- when you were working elsewhere I just want to establish where you were in fact during September.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of September, I suppose, I was out, but it says until September, but the work described in that first sentence would have been based in Turbe and Travnik, and it would be about the convoys of Muslims and Croats coming from the Prijedor-Banja Luka region into Central Bosnia, on, as I explained, along the route that I myself had taken some weeks prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I understand that. Then after you had done that, you took some time off, and the question is simply where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: After -- during September, when I -- in between the two visits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Rome -- or Milan, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Somewhere in Italy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. Now, then, you came back then in October of 1992, came back to --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And you gave evidence about certain events that occurred during that period. And then I think you left between November of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, when you came back to make the film.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would make sense, as far as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Right. And you spent two months, I think, making the -- making the film or being involved with that, and then you were absent until July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: January, February, March. That's correct, as I recall, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: When you spent a week in Vitez, I think?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before going down to Herzegovina, July, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And then as we heard more recently, today, you returned to Bosnia in September of 1993, which is when you visited East Mostar, I think, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Bosnia, yes. I spent some time in Croatia late -- or in Zagreb late August. Early September, late August, yes, I was back in Bosnia around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, let me -- let me then just turn to one or two other things before I hand over to my colleagues. You testified yesterday about conversations you had had with a man by the name of Pero Markovic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I sought to have a conversation -- this is the mayor of Capljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I sought to have a conversation with him on the day I went to Capljina in 1992, but we didn't speak, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you had a conversation regarding his activities.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: About him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: About him, yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was with people from the UNHCR. I had never met him, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I understand, but you did have a conversation with officials of the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: From which you gathered that Mr. Markovic had a reputation of being somewhat extreme.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they said, yes. He was also named by the people in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And his function, I think, you were told, was that he was the mayor and also the head of the local HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both. The mayor, I certainly recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And based on the information that you received, you formed the opinion, did you not, that it was Pero Markovic who was the moving force behind the expulsions in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the impression I got from the UNHCR, yes. I mean, they -- well, they didn't -- I mean, they didn't rate him very highly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No. I understand. And as a result of what you were told, you -- that was a view that you accepted, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I mean, I'd never met him. I'd been told what I was told. Whether I accepted it or not, I mean, I wouldn't have written -- I didn't accept it to the point of writing it, but what he -- what was said about him was enough to cause considerable alarm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, indeed, as I say, his name had been mentioned by the people in Capljina as well as the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And you certainly had no reason to disbelieve what you'd been told.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If I may have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions for Mr. Vulliamy at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, my client would like to put some questions where he was somehow more or less more acquainted with the facts, and if you permit, that first he put some questions and I would then follow up. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vulliamy, we don't have much time, so please try to answer briefly and precisely.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You mentioned visiting the Dretelj camp on the 8th or 9th of August 1992. There were Serbs detained in the camp and HOS members controlled the camp.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know whether HOS was not under the influence of the political structure of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact relationship. I know that they were associated with a political party based in Zagreb but I don't know their exact relationship to the community of Herceg-Bosna. I do know that at that time they had a fairly antagonistic relationship with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Could we therefore conclude that when a political party has an army, it is not under the influence of any sort of social organisation that would be part of the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the relationship between the community and the HOS was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did HOS have a headquarters of its own?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it had an overall headquarters but it had a headquarters --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Please, if you don't know the answer, just say I don't know and we can then move on.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a headquarters for the area in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the HOS commander, Blaz Kraljevic, who was later killed, was appointed as a general by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were more Muslims than Croats in the HOS?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there were Muslims in the HOS, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers the HOS units had in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and as far as Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a figure, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part I saw them with Kalashnikov weapons. I didn't see much sign of artillery. In fact, not any, but Kalashnikovs certainly and other small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of institution is there in the HZ HB, a military and political institution if it can tolerate the HOS army but can't control it in any way?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, forgive me, sir, I didn't understand the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is the HZ HB as an organisational structure important if, in addition to the regular army, there is another army faction that it cannot control in any way?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unaware of what the law of the H -- of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is as regarding what armed forces were or weren't legal at that time. What I did know was that the HVO and the armija BH were fighting in alliance. Where HOS fitted into that alliance, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the HOS was in favour of a Bosnia and Herzegovina as an integral part of Croatia which would extend as far as the Drina.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what was explained to me by Mr. Dedakovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Isn't the idea of having a Croatia up to the Drina, isn't this the idea of the Independent State of Croatia and of Ante Pavelic, an idea in which -- as a result of which the Muslims were expelled as part of that entity?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that that was -- that the HOS wanted to repeat the border of 1941, yes. That was also explained to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: As a journalist, were you interested in the fact that Alija Izetbegovic appointed a general of such an army?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that the -- is it Kraljevic, the man who was killed at the roadblock, I didn't know that he was also a general in the armija BH. I knew his name - I had never met him - as the, until then, commander of the HOS. I didn't know that he was also a general in the armija BH, if he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Dretelj camp was dismantled through the HVO armed forces and they risked a conflict with the HOS? And I'm referring to the Dretelj camp in 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know what the risk was when there is a Serbian aggression? Do you know what the risk was of a possible conflict breaking out between the HVO and the HOS?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was by then aware -- or, no, I wasn't actually, sorry. With hindsight, I'm aware of the risk of a conflict between any forces on what was being called the free territory while there was fighting going on against the Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who issued an order to a group of individuals according to which the Dretelj camp should be dismantled by use of force, the Dretelj camp in which Serbs were detained?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who gave the HVO order? No, I don't. I didn't know that the camp had been closed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I was the person responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought your previous question might lead to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there something that you think would be incorrect or immoral in Mate Boban's statement according to which the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina should refer not only to citizens but also to the rights of peoples; the Croats, the Muslims, and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, do I think that that's wrong for him to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, do you think it's wrong?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's up to him whether it's right or wrong. I was by now getting a little weary of this constant not verbal use but deployment of the word "narod" because I'd come across it too much in Croatia and from the Bosnian Serbs, and I was uncomfortable with this constant emphasis on the collective right of the "narod." I'm not saying it's wrong, I'm just saying that, in my experience, it had led to some unfortunate and very violent action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Muslims, Croats and Serbs, are they constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina and do they have sovereign rights?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the break-up of Yugoslavia or before? Under the constitution? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Under the constitution and as a people, or as peoples.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that when -- that before the break-up of Yugoslavia, the "narod" did exist as groups within the former Yugoslavia, and I'm aware that the "Muslimanski narod" became a "narod" in this way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is the right to defence and to freedom an obligation and the right of a sovereign people and of the individuals or members of a particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've given the accused some leeway here in terms of his cross-examination but really this is not the best witness to be putting these questions to. They call for opinions. This is a journalist. He's testified about what he observed, people he spoke with, what he saw. This is well beyond the scope of his direct examination, in the first place. Second of all, it calls for opinions; and in the third place, it's not a proper basis for cross-examining. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The witness was drawing conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, if I may briefly respond. I think it's well within the testimony we heard yesterday and well within the scope of the gentleman's knowledge, because he is drawing a distinction. He's saying "narod," you know, nations, and he's only saying that there are two. Now he's acknowledging that there is a third one, and I think it -- and Mr. Praljak or anyone else here is entitled to set up the situation for other witnesses to follow. The gentleman was in the field. He's written a book. He's drawn conclusions. Assumingly, one would know what he's talking about, so I think it's well within the scope and I would insist that Mr. Praljak be allowed to continue in this vein. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could be heard on one additional issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure if this is the appropriate time to be raising this issue, Mr. President, but Mr. Karnavas represents another accused in this case and we might be needing some guidelines here in a multiple accused, multiply-represented situation. Again, if Mr. Karnavas thinks these are appropriate questions, perhaps, given his legal training, he can formulate questions that are not objectionable when it's his opportunity to cross-examine the witness. The Prosecution does, however, object to this type of intervention by someone who does not represent Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
