utterances.text: I'm entitled, Your Honour, to make my record, and if I can assist anyone else, I don't see a problem with that. If the Court wishes to give me some guidance, that's fine. But I think that in the event I have some information or some knowledge that might be of assistance to General Praljak or anyone else, I don't see the reason why I should not. If I'm told by his counsel not to intervene, that's very well but I think that -- I don't want to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The question that the Judges put to themselves, having heard Mr. Praljak's questions, is whether this is pertinent and whether the witness is the right person to answer questions of a political nature and questions that have to do with constitutional matters. Before I authorise you to continue putting your questions, there is something that the witness should clarify for the Chamber. Sir, as a journalist, are you an investigative journalist or a political journalist? Since, as you're well aware, there are different types of journalists. There are journalists who use facts and on the basis of facts write articles of a political nature. They refer to the constitution, to people, to other such ideas, and then we have journalists who are more interested in facts; they go into the field, they observe that there is a concentration camp there and they explain that there are inmates in the camp. They don't ask any other questions. Mr. Praljak's questions have to do with the political context, so there are references to Mate Boban, to certain other matters such as the constitution. In order to avoid wasting time, given the objections we have heard, would you say that you're qualified to answer the questions put to you? If you believe that you are not qualified to answer these questions, please inform us of the fact and Mr. Praljak will move on to another area. Naturally, you should avoid expressing your own personal opinion because, as a journalist, well, you write for an important British newspaper, and this would be the newspaper's point of view. So do you think you would be able to answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do so easily. I have never been a reporter of, if you like, party politics or a political correspondent. I have done investigations, as into corruption or whatever. Covering war is -- or conflict, which I've also done, is closer to your latter category than the former. On the other hand, you have, I think, to know a bit about the political situation, although my detailed knowledge of the constitution, there are certainly better qualified people to discuss that than me, but I am aware of this, as counsel referred to, the two "narod," Srpski and Hrvatski, in that country. I don't think I ever said there were only two because I did know that, under the former Yugoslavia, a third category was added, "Muslimanski narod," and -- but I'm not an expert on constitutional politics nor have I ever been a party political correspondent or a constitutional correspondent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, the journalist has just said that there is a field he's not familiar with, so please try to put more precise questions to the witness, questions that the witness can answer. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You said that Mate Boban mentioned Switzerland as a model for Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is Switzerland a good example of a way in which a country should be organised if it has three peoples?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really have a view on Switzerland in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is it true that you never heard Mate Boban say anything about Herceg-Bosna seceding and being annexed to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He never used the word "annexation" or "secession," but he gave the impression that he wanted there to be very close ties. He used the terms "cultural," "spiritual," and I think "material" or "economic," and certainly the border between Herceg-Bosna and Croatia at that time was almost non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, please try to answer my questions and it's not necessary to tell us about your impressions. Please just answer my questions. Impressions are for the Judges. If it's true that Mate Boban and Croatia signed Cutileiro's and Vance-Owen's plans and all the plans drafted by the international community, wouldn't it be illogical for them to wish to go to war at the same time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's logical or not. They were manifestly preparing to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: To go to war to fight an aggression, yes. Would it be logical to assume that those who wanted war and wanted to conquer territory were those who did not sign plans or proposals drawn up by the international community?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as I'm aware, and you mentioned the Vance-Owen Plan, which more or less duplicated what Mate Boban had outlined he wanted, so far as I know, the same people were signing the Vance-Owen Plan as were also talking about the HVO being the civilian military authority in the area and implying, at least, that they had some sort of control over the HVO, and I think at some point, yes, Mr. Boban did say that the Croatian people, and the HVO is their army, were armed and ready to defend their freedom, which, as I think I testified, in my experience by then defence didn't always mean a defence, although in some cases it might well have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mate Boban, when you expected him to talk about his success against the Serbs in the summer of 1992, also spoke to you about political problems and you were surprised. Was a political solution for the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina a basis for war or a basis for peace?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What surprised me was how little he wanted to talk about dealings with the Serbs, given that that's who -- I presumed he and his allies on -- in the Bosnian Muslim and government side were fighting, but I didn't see his discourse as a plea for peace. I saw it as more a sturdy assertion of these rights of the "narod" we've been talking about, with references to armed force, if necessary, which he implied he thought it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. In Grude you saw some cars with HV number plates. Do you know how many people born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how many citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, participated in the defence of Croatia when it was attacked in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many, but I know there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we conclude that it would be logical for them to come and defend their family members and their homes in Bosnia and Herzegovina after four UNPAs were formed in Croatia and a truce was established at the beginning of 1992 in that area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would one say, could one say that it's logical that people from Bosnia-Herzegovina who participated in the fight in the Croatian army to defend Croatia from the Serbian aggression, could one say that it's logical for them to come to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the truce in Croatia to defend their homes there and to defend their family members there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. You have some knowledge of the military. Wouldn't it be illogical to calm the tensions in the battlefield in Croatia and then allow the same aggressor, who was the same objectives, to move all his military power to Bosnia and Herzegovina and to continue doing everything that he had already done in Vukovar, et cetera? Is it possible to distinguish these two ideas? Can we calm the situation in one area and continue in another area? We have the same aggressor, the same army, the same forces. Is that logical?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware of the remobilisation, as you put it, of the former JNA, now basically the Serbian army, and Bosnian Serbian army, and I'm also aware - and it wasn't just me - that the HV, as you said, rallied to this second war in Bosnia. It wasn't just me who saw their vehicles. In fact, the military monitors saw them and their weaponry quite regularly. We used to be briefed up to and including the siege of Mostar, East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: How many cars with HV number plates did you see in Grude?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Grude at that particular time, I don't recall an exact number. They were there and they were present throughout the period we have been talking about across the area. Not in very large numbers but I don't want to put a figure to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would it be possible for the young men from the Croatian army to take a vehicle and go to places that had been attacked, places where their family members lived, without authorisation? Would it be possible for them to do this without authorisation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Reference was made to 1992, in the summer. Boban said he wouldn't allow the Muslims to participate in the government in Mostar and elsewhere in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation that I recall referred specifically to Mostar. I don't remember him saying it about the whole territory, but in Mostar he said there would be no legal Muslim representation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it then possible to explain the fact that the ABiH was arming itself constantly in Mostar right up to the beginning of the conflict, given that Boban was the Supreme Commander of the army?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that the Bosnian army in Mostar was armed, of course. I was discussing their allied operation with the Serbs with the HVO. I have to admit I don't know whether Boban was regarded as the commander of the Bosnian army in Herceg-Bosna. Whether he regarded himself as that or not, I don't know. But I -- as far as I know, the Bosnian army was not under his command. When I visit the Mostar in August, 1992, of course the Bosnian army was armed, and I was aware of that, and it was fighting an alliance with the HVO which was also armed. I have to say I don't know what the chain of command was between Mr. Boban and the armija BH in Mostar, the formal chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm interested in logics. If somebody wishes to subject somebody and provides him with weapons all the time, then this -- is it not a logical paradox?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. To --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, would you please ask questions that the witness can answer. Because with the kind of questions that you're asking now, you are pleading your own case. We haven't reached that point in the trial yet. This witness had the privilege of meeting Mr. Boban, so it would be interesting to ask him questions about the nature of the contacts he had with him, not political speculations or things like that. And the journalist has told you a number of times that he doesn't know. His answer was that he didn't know. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know this, that in May, 1992, the whole of the left bank of the River Neretva, from north Mostar up to the very border with Croatia, was ethnically cleansed of the Serb aggression?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that there was a battle for Mostar in July, which was won by the Muslim-Croat alliance, but I'm also aware that the Serbs in their advance on the -- by "left," I think you mean the east bank of the Neretva -- had ethnically cleansed Croats and Muslims from that area who had come into West Mostar. Indeed, I spoke to some of them during that visit in August, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Where did all these refugees go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had come into -- into Mostar. I don't know how long they stayed there, but the ones that I met, who had, as you say, been ethnically cleansed by the Serbs from the east bank of the Neretva and from as far as Trebinje, I don't know where they went after Mostar, except that when I returned to Mostar in October, 1992, many of them were still there because most of them were the ones I was referring to when I said that they were required by the new rules in force to re-register with the HVO authorities. They were mostly from that east bank that you've been referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, you seem to have the opinion all the time that Mate Boban and politics wished to engage in war against the Muslims, to expel the Muslims and to gain supremacy over the Muslims. That's how I understand your conclusions to be. Would that be a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Expel," he didn't use those words, but what I saw in Prozor made me wonder. "Supremacy over" within the territory of Herceg-Bosna, definitely yes. And sorry, what was your other -- there was another -- oh, "declare war on." I thought his attitude -- I thought he was taking a fairly bellicose stand with regard to the authority of the Sarajevo government, yes. But you've used three categories there. I'd agree with two of them. I'm not sure about "expel."

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you be more precise when answering my questions, please. How, then, can you explain the following fact: That in 1993, in April, in areas which had already been cleansed, we have the whole 4th Corps of the BH army and all the refugees have returned, and expelled persons, and the Muslim Bregava Brigade in Stolac? How did they return? Who armed them? And is that not a contradiction to the desire for ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's an incredibly compound question, and again, he -- there is elements of this question that are not -- there are elements that are not in evidence. There are elements of this question that are incredibly complex and compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. You're asking a question which has several facets to it. Try and break it up, break the question up in such a way that you can receive a specific answer, because otherwise, the Prosecutor is going to stand up and object. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In May, 1992, you have the whole left bank of the River Neretva cleansed. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there but I read about it and I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. In June, 1992, the liberated territory, liberated from the Serb occupation, is that correct or not? Was it or was it not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was July. I wasn't there. I stand corrected if it was June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, all right, July. All the refugees, of the brigade, were returned, sent back. Yes or no. Those who wanted to return.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you mean the refugees from the east bank returned to the east Serbian-controlled territory? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. On the eastern side now, which was under the control of the Serbs, we had the establishment of the 4th Corps of the BH army, and in Stolac the Brigade called Bregava Brigade. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the 4th Corps of the BH army was in alliance on the east bank, as you said. I've never heard of the Bregava Brigade, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Could that have been done without the active participation of the HVO, both the civilian and the military component?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the deployment of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And the refugees.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it at that point. No, I don't think it could have done because I kept saying as far as I know the armies were fighting in alliance at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to be as brief as possible, Your Honours, to save time. Was Jajce linked to Travnik with a narrow corridor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And a very frightening one along which I tried to go many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On the left and right side of the corridor, you had Serb units. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On the left side, behind the Serb lines, if you know, did you have the BH army units there at Komar hill? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might well have done at the time with maps in front of me. I have to say I can't recall exactly what was on the other side of those Serbian lines now. This must be towards Bugojno. I don't know who held the territory but I think it was probably both BiH and HVO, but I'm afraid I can't answer your question at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you happen to know of a single attempt by the BH army from Bugojno to expand the corridor by attacking the Serb forces from the rear? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I heard about that but I wasn't there for it. I think there were various attempts to expand the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the following, that from Zagreb doctors were sent with an armoured vehicle, a bus, to pull out the wounded from Jajce; Doctors Kveric [phoen], Barisic [phoen], et cetera?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but it doesn't surprise me. There was some heroic stuff going up and down that corridor by both the HVO and the BH armija to service Jajce and to rescue the wounded. Doesn't surprise me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know that all the wounded, regardless of ethnicity, were pulled out and for the most part transported to the HVO hospital in Bugojno? Do you know about that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but again I'm quite prepared to believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many units we sent from Herzegovina to reinforce and assist Jajce when we came to understand that its position was very bad? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically -- sorry, specifically about units from Herzegovina but I know that the HVO was, like the Bosnian army, trying to get people through that corridor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know that not a single unit that was sent to assist Jajce arrived in Jajce? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I was about to say I don't know -- I mean, whether they got there is another matter because it -- it's a very difficult --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know that all the units were stopped by the BH army forces between Vakuf and Travnik, Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, I just -- [overlapping microphones] when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And do you know that we sent a HOS unit where there was 70 per cent Muslims to help out Jajce, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about HOS in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know that that particular unit was stopped by the BH army and held for three days under siege and that it never reached Jajce?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about the HOS. I told you I didn't know about the HOS going to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Judges to my left and my right and I myself -- although I myself have a different opinion, are -- think that you're asking questions that are not pertinent, and the majority of judges would like you to concentrate on questions which the witness can answer and contribute to our knowledge of what he saw, so that he can answer questions on the basis of what he saw or knew about. The previous question that you just asked him was a speculative question, and it is not useful to us. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You mentioned the Diamont Road.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you said that that road was constructed by English engineering units.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said part of it was enhanced or tarmacked by, where necessary. I didn't say the whole road was built by them, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That route was one through which hundreds of thousands of refugees passed. And now just finally, let me ask you this: In your statement you say that you received from me permission to visit the collection centre, the camp in Dretelj, on the 8th of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be -- I'm sure your date is right. I recognise you from that, that moment, and so far as I'm aware, it was you who gave us permission verbally and, to the best of my knowledge in a paper, an order paper, to go to Dretelj, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yesterday, in a document that was shown to the Court, we saw that President Franjo Tudjman sent a letter to Mate Boban on the 6th of September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the letter I think I recall reading in Slobodna Dalmacija on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You said that the probable reason for that letter was pressure on the part of the international community and threats of sanction to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, an objection was raised to that - to quote counsel - analysis, which was upheld. I'm not sure if I'm obliged to comment. All I can say is that, on reading that letter, one was aware that this discourse was being had at diplomatic levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You also said in your statement that you were the first journalist to enter the collection centre, the Dretelj camp. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, we were the first group of journalists to go, but if there is a published article by somebody about Dretelj prior to our visit, then obviously my view at that point was incorrect. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the court for my order of the 1st of September 1993 to be displayed, giving permission that in Gabela camp or for a TV, German TV crew ZDF German TV crew to enter Gabela camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, this document was last in our batch which we put electronically and we just discovered that the last document for some reason is not in the electronic system, so I would like to use the copies and then probably through the morning it will come into the system. I have four copies; one should be for Trial Chamber, one for witness, for ELMO, and -- I'm expecting this document to be released during the morning. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is this not six days before Franjo Tudjman sent the letter to Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this was broadcast over television, is it not possible that it was only then that people in Croatia learned of the actual situation in those camps and that that included Franjo Tudjman too?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to suppose when or how people in Croatia found out about the conditions in the camp, nor have I seen the film, nor was I aware of it. But you may have a point. I don't know about this film. I only said that we were the first into Dretelj because it was the commander of the man in Dretelj who said that we were. I didn't know about Gabela and I didn't know about this film, but I do agree it was before the date of the letter, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the easier identification of the document, I would like to state on the record that this document number is 3D 00141 so later we can identify it and I will then ask you to admit the document. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, so the warden told you that you were the first journalist to enter Dretelj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it was the commander of the camp who told us we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't know whether that was actually true or not.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no reason to doubt him, and as I say I didn't know about this prior visit by German journalists to Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 7th of September 1993, a journalist from Globus by the name of Zeljko Rogosic had received permission from me, an order, granting permission for him to enter both Gabela and Dretelj, and that he did so after encountering a certain amount of problems?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew neither that he'd been, nor about the [unintelligible].

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Can you tell me why you were surprised when you received permission from me to enter the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was gratefully surprised, because people working with Mr. Boban had been quite emphatic, indeed on the day that you mentioned just now, the 7th, and back in July, that we couldn't go to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you ever meet me before that date?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'd never seen you before that date. I knew your face from the newspapers. I'd never seen you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Although I would have a lot more to ask you, I'll rest there. Thank you for answering the questions, and thank you to the Trial Chamber for allowing me to ask them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I am defence counsel for Mr. Praljak, and I have a few more questions to ask you in respect of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yesterday you spoke about your travels through Prozor, so first of all let's locate and pinpoint what this was about. On page 53 of the transcript, line 12 to 14, and 53, line 21, you said that after meeting with Boban on the 24th of October - that is to say the meeting with Boban was on the 24th of October - you travelled towards the north of Bosnia, to Travnik and Vitez, and all this with respect to the critical situation in Jajce, and you mentioned that a moment ago today.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there was also, in between that, there was, I think I mentioned, an excursion with UNPROFOR soldiers to try and locate a route through to Sarajevo but when I was coming down through Prozor, it was after going up into Central Bosnia to check the latest situation with regard to Jajce. That's as I recall, yes, and I think I testified to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You've now incorporated that into the long story that we heard from you yesterday. So we know where we stand. But you're not quite sure whether or not you were moving northwards towards Travnik and if you passed through the town of Prozor on the 24th or the 25th, but you did say that you do remember that it was a weekend; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that I was driving southwards in the first of those drives, yes, when it was, as I said I think, normal -- it was -- it was a Friday or a Saturday, I think I said Friday or Saturday possibly -- I think it was a Friday afternoon or a Saturday but I just -- I honestly can't remember exactly which but it was driving south definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] But that means on your return way from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm confusing you. I will continue in Croatian -- or in English.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, from Central Bosnia down towards Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was a little bit different than you said -- than you stated yesterday. Yesterday I understood -- and I was checking the transcript. I understood that during that weekend, which was immediately after your meeting with Boban, and you were quite certain that a meeting with Boban took place on 24. What you were not certain and, of course, after certain years, is that whether you were travelling north toward Travnik on the very same day or next day, and then you said, Well, it must have been during the weekend.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it was during the weekend, and I was travelling south through Prozor the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for the first time, but the first time in that episode.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. I appreciate that, sir. But then, if you think that you were driving in direction south, so you are on your returning trip from Travnik down to Herzegovina, that is highly impossible because you said that on 24 you met Boban down there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Grude, on south. You went to Vitez and Travnik, and on the other place, a little bit after on those pages, you said, "I was going back in two or three days." So that then must be, let's say, 26, 27. But anyway, I don't think it's so important. What is important is that you said on the first time - and that is the substance - on my first journey toward north, I passed through Prozor and it was a peaceful atmosphere, nothing was happening there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, first journey was south, southwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But then how come you came on the north in order to go back to the south?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left the British and moved up into Central Bosnia, as I recall, through Kiseljak, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So some other way, not through Prozor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going up north before coming down through Prozor, but I can't remember the route, I think through Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then whatever direction it was, you said during that weekend, 24 --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. It might be 24, 25, here, somewhere.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which day is which date. It was Friday, Saturday or Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. But nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were going to church, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you're claiming that at that journey, first time when you came in Prozor, it was peaceful atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then only couple of days later, what, two or three days later --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was a hell there.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. Well, sir, let me introduce you some documents, and I think it will be helpful for the Court in further proceedings, not only related to that, but since you started it, I should -- we have to go to that. I am calling document 3D 00124 to be on the screen, please. While we are waiting for the document, I will just point out short description. This is a document issued on 24/10. It is issued by municipal authorities, Tactical Group 1, of Jablanica, and the document is rather lengthy. It has full two pages. It is signed by Commander Salko Zeren, which is, by the name, Muslim, and it is issued obviously by the unit belonging to army. And in the opening paragraph, the document says: "Pursuant to the oral query of the Main Staff head deputy, on sending armed forces Jablanica unit to Prozor, we report you on the following: During night, the units -- the unit was ready to move, but was not sent from the following reasons." And now I don't think we have to read all that in this particular moment, but then somewhere on the end, he furtherly explained that: "Our unit could not perform the task for the reason of strong HVO forces concentration, establishment degree, and equipment of the same unit. The same unit -" meaning this one - "would have suffered huge losses if there had been such a unit engagement in order to close the communication and disable the evacuation of refugees and wounded persons from Prozor." Et cetera, et cetera. So it obviously shows that on those days, particularly 24 October and obviously sometime before that, so day or two days before that, there is engagement, there is a kind of conflict between those two forces. And let's see how this situation developed further. I would call document 3D 00123. Sir, I would show you just a couple of documents and then would ask for a comment related to time and then probably to events because --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- in the next couple of days, you saw some portion of the events.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the document issued by HVO on 23rd October, so one day before the previous document. And it is an information and letters signed by commander of HVO Prozor, and also signed by president of HVO, meaning civilian authorities in Prozor, and addressed to military and civilian representatives of Muslims of municipality of Prozor, on 23rd October. Subject matter: Our proposals for overcoming the newly arising political and security situation.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see what you're reading, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is on the first page of the translation, so one page back.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I would ask you to pay attention to particularly, for example, for on item 1, [Microphone not activated] they demanding urgent and unconditional cessation of all military operations. So I guess we can comfortably conclude that something was going on. And they are specifically demanding withdrawal of all armed units from the town and they also implies that they are [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- army units there. Then I would call the next document, the number being 3D 00122. Unfortunately, it's also a rather lengthy document of two pages. Again -- well, I have to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, when you give the number of the document, are you actually giving us the number that's at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now directing the Defence to the following: When giving the number of the document, it has to be the number under which the electronic version of the document was filed, not an internal Defence number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I was referring to wrong numbers. Both are in the system but I was not yet trained on that. However, I guess that court officer and my case manager were successful in finding a proper one, even though I cited the wrong number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vulliamy, this document once again is dated the 23rd, which was definitely before the time when you travelled through the area. This is once again a document coming from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Main Staff, and its forward command post in Konjic. I would like to direct you to item 3 of the document, where the tasks of the units are described, and on the following page, on page 2, under item 3/3, we see the task of the municipal defence staff of Prozor municipality. And in that paragraph, the person who signed the document, Jovan Divjak, says as follows: "Defend firmly current positions and upon arrival of the battalion of the Jablanica municipality staff, prevent seizing of Prozor and undertake measures in order to move the forces or repel forces from Prozor municipality. In discussions with the HVO staff, find measures in order to solve the existing situation." Without going into reading the entire document, and we have it in its entirety here, but without doing that, we can see that some activities were already taking place, and clearly it was happening before this date, the 23rd of October. Although I have many more documents to show you, I have just one more to tender right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like document number 3D 040016. Yeah. That is the document. I'm sorry, it's not yet on the screen, this screen. We have it here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kovacic, could I kindly ask you to systematically quote what you call the prenumbering system, which does not bear any 04 number but rather the 3D 00 whatever followed by 3 digits. That would simplify everybody's life. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is the number which I cited previously in previous situation. The judge is giving me signs that he has the document. Yes. That is the document. So this is 3D 00125. Perhaps while we are waiting for the document -- and it is on the screen, okay, it is very short document. Now, this time it is HVO document signed by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, that time brigadier, and I think it's sufficiently short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So based on this document, once again it is clear, it was also issued on the 24th of October, General Petkovic here asks that contacts be established with the warring party. That indicates that something was under way. And then he says that unconditional cease-fire be negotiated. Once again this indicates that the conflict is in progress. And then he orders that movements of units from outside of the conflict area be halted. That is to say units coming to the conflict area, any units. And then he says that truce ought to be established and practically he stops any type of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be appropriate time and then we conclude this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's 12.05 now. We will have a break, which will enable the witness to rest and recuperate, and we shall continue with our work at 13.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would kindly ask the court officer to remove the document from the screen which is now on the screen, which is 5D 636. I think that is a document which belongs to Mr. Jonjic, and he will use it later. The last document we have seen on the screen was D 00125 and we are now going to next document and then I will close this story with the documents, but I would like to use this witness to see the one, since it is connected to the Prozor October event. This is document 00137, so 3D 00137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, could you please give us the number at the bottom of the page. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to ask court officer -- it is not the document I requested. I asked the document 3D 00137. Okay. So I'm sorry, I just warn that this is the English version of the document. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vulliamy, you can see based on this document that it's the document of the Croatian Defence Council, command of the Rama Brigade, the 5th of November, 1992. And then can we see who signed the document, please? It was signed by several persons: President of the commission, Mijo Jozic, who signed it on behalf of the HVO; commander of the Rama Brigade, Ilija Ramic; and operations officer in the Brigade, Tomislav. All of them members of the HVO. Based on the heading, we can see that this report was drafted at the request of the Main Staff of the HVO, pursuant to order 2437/92, and the subheading, or rather, the subject of this report are causes for the conflict between the HVO and TO. This pertains to Prozor. This is quite an extensive document detailing the chronology of the relations between the HVO and the TO, Territorial Defence, starting in March of 1992. I'm going to skip over that and could we please look at item 4 on page 3 of the document. In the English version, this is on page 5. English version page 5. And then further down, yes, yes, we have item 4 here. So here in this paragraph, they summarise the consequences of the conflict in terms of casualties, those who were killed and wounded on both sides, as well as damage to facilities. We can see that 11 were dead on the BH army side, 5 on the HVO side, 18 wounded members of the HVO, and unknown number of wounded members of the TO, and some of them hospitalised in the war hospital in Rumboci, and so on. So let us conclude with this. Let me explain to you why I wanted you to see these documents. Mr. Vulliamy, do you agree that the dates given by you, the 24th and the 25th, so when you were in Prozor for the first time, when it was still calm, those can't be accurate dates because, as we established based on this, a serious conflict erupted between the two armies as early as the 23rd. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that there were mobilisations from your prior documents, which I'm in no position to dispute. I have tried during the break to clarify the time line. And although I can't give you a precise date of when I made the southbound drive through Prozor, all I can say is that I did not see any of these hostilities and the place appeared to be normal, but I can -- I can help you further with the time line of my whereabouts now or at any point that you want. Shall I do that now? Or do you want me to -- or do you want me to talk about the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, no, thank you. But to conclude this topic, it is certain, regardless of the dates, and it's natural that after 13 years it's difficult for you to specify dates, regardless of which itinerary you had, whether you were going north or going south, regardless of the route you took, so it is obvious that starting on the 23rd and then on the 24th and 25th, the events there were quite intense and you saw what was happening there regardless of whether it was two or three days before or after. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree with regard to at least the area visible from the main street of Prozor itself. In order to help you and the Court, I've taken the liberty - and I hope this is in order - to make a call to the library at the Guardian, and I'm very happy for my phone to be checked for you all to ensure that that's the only communication I've made, simply in order to -- and this pertains to our discussion at the end of yesterday, that we don't have the dates of articles which are readily available to everybody else on the internet outside this courtroom, and I thought that in the interests of helping the Court, it would help if I could give you the dates of three articles to clear up this time line. I spoke to a researcher called Linda McDonald - you're welcome to check that - and anyway, what I have is that the date that the article about the firefight in Novi Travnik was published - published - was the morning of the 24th of October. The date when my article on the events I discussed earlier with Mostar I presume to include the interview with Mr. Boban, although I didn't ask Ms. McDonald for details of the articles, I just wanted the dates, was the 26th of October; and the first article on Prozor was after a northbound drive, and that was on the 28th of October. And that would have been sent from Travnik, as I think I explained in my testimony, on the night of what I now imagine -- and I'm just trying to help with the time line here -- would have been the night of the 27th. I can't give you a date, precise date, for my southbound drive through Prozor when everything was, as I said, fairly normal, but I can give you the likely date of when I drove back up northwards, and that would seem to be the 27th; that is to say, the day before the publication of that first article. I will stand by my testimony that I saw no sign of hostilities from the main road or near the main road on that southbound journey, which must have been between the 26th -- well, it probably was the 26th, but I absolutely stand by my testimony that the dramatic contrast between the relative calm, or indeed the normality of the southbound drive contrasted very dramatically and suddenly with what we found when we drove back up north on what I'm taking to be from this the 27th. Of course I note what is in your documents, but there was no sign of fighting let alone heavy fighting when I made the southbound drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the additional explanation. I think that now we have clarified all this in a way. However, this begs a question: In view of the amount of time you spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the events you witnessed, on the basis of the explanation you just gave us, and bearing in mind that you went through a town on a certain day and you didn't notice any traces of combat and then three days later you saw them, in the meantime, we see based on documents that there have been some combat activities, some fighting, even when it was not obvious to the naked eye of a traveller going through a town. Can we, based on that, conclude that sometimes, even when one is on the ground, one cannot gather and convey the most reliable information?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You gather and convey the most reliable information you can. If there was fighting away from that main street, I didn't see it. If you asked me to ratify my testimony that there were civilians out on the street and people coming out of church, which is why I thought it was the weekend, which it doesn't appear to be, I'm sorry, I was not prepared to give a precise date for that southbound drive, then I will ratify that testimony that there was no sign of any hostility of anything like the traces of which we saw when we drove back north. Nor was there any sign of the expulsion of civilians which clearly was the case when we returned the following day, which I take to be the 28th, and I imagine, although I didn't ask Ms. McDonald at the Guardian, there will be a further article about when we found the people in the hillsides. As regards the veracity of this itinerary, I can, if you like, give you the names and organisations of all the people I was travelling with. I was not working alone, so that you can verify any of those dates and reports in publications other than my own by people other than myself, or speak to them, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vulliamy, thank you for your extensive explanation. Essentially, at least in the first portion of your answer, we reached precisely the conclusion that I expressed to you, that when one passes through a town, one doesn't necessarily know everything that's going on there or in the vicinity behind a hill, just two or three kilometres away. That's my point. But let's leave that aside.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, that -- that's a point but it begs -- it's a question too. You can, by driving through a town, see the difference between the main street of that town when people are out on the streets, civilians, and shopping and in cafes, and when you return back through that town and large numbers of buildings have been incinerated and attacked by shell and small arms fire. That you can see very clearly by passing through the town, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that we are not communicating properly. First you confirm that, yes, sometimes one cannot see everything, and in some other situations, yes, it's obvious that you can see that, and I think that you and I fully agree. This stems from the discussion we just had.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's agree that you can't see everything, and nor did, on that southbound journey, I venture into the hinterland between Prozor and Jablanica or any other hinterland, but can we also agree that you can tell a difference between a main street on -- upon which there has been a lot of shooting and shelling and incineration and a main street when there isn't, and I noticed that difference during those two drives through the town in opposite directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave that there. I think we've clarified the matter. There is just one other minor detail I would like to mention. You have just mentioned the entire situation once again. Now it appears that this occurred two or three days subsequent to the date initially provided, and I don't mean to say anything negative when I point this out, this happened a long time ago, but on that day when you saw those refugees there. You don't know why they were in the streets, you don't know what the reason was for their presence in the streets, you didn't know who they were fleeing from, why they were fleeing, you had no reliable information about the matter at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they gave us their account of why they were there, and that was what I published. I was not, as you rightly say, in Prozor when that attack took place or when they fled, but I was talking to them a fairly small distance outside the town shortly after they had fled. Again, precise date, well, I can be quite precise, I think. If my first article filed from Travnik was published on the 28th, then it must have been on that day that I encountered them because we went, as I think I testified, straight back down in pursuit of the -- or in search of the reported 5.000 Muslims who had gone missing from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me rephrase my question. Apart from what you testified about yesterday, and you have repeated part of your testimony today, the only sources you had with regard to these refugees is what you in fact found out from them in the course of two or three brief conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a number -- a number of conversations that weren't so brief, actually. We spent quite a bit of time up in those hills, and I also, I think, testified that on the road back to Tomislavgrad that night, we were caught in a small convoy, medium-sized convoy of troops, returning to Tomislavgrad and had the conversation with the HVO commander who told us that Prozor was now clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. This is something that we can see in the documents. It's not necessary to go into that now. Since you have mentioned the name of this lady in the Guardian, do you think you could fax those articles to the Court since the Prosecution says they do not have copies of the articles?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which articles are these, sorry, the lady?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The articles you mentioned with regard to the conversation that you had with the lady from the Guardian. You said that you phoned her, you said you did that two minutes ago and you said she provided you with the dates.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: She provided me with the dates, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you get back to London, do you think you could fax those articles to the Chamber, to the Court?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have them either faxed -- everything is done electronically nowadays. I could have them e-mailed, to any address you give me, at the first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible for your office to send them to us today? Let's leave that matter aside. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd be very grateful if that were possible. Just one other minor detail with regard to Prozor, and with regard to your testimony about the events in Prozor yesterday, well, we saw a video, a short video. P 1784 was the exhibit number. I'm not sure that I understood the discussion that followed that. After having seen the video, you said that you weren't sure whether this occurred in October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I'll explain as quickly as I can. I made the film during the early part of 1993, as I've explained. The producer of the film did the editing back in London while I was getting on with my work. That footage was chosen by her from the BBC archives and, as far as they are concerned, labelled Prozor during those events. I think I commented on that yesterday. The street looked as I recalled it. The soldiers, I think I, if I recall rightly, said they looked more sort of ruffian than I remember and they didn't have the red ribbons, but that -- the BBC archive chose those pictures while I wasn't in London, while they were editing, putting together the film. That's all I can say with regard to that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vulliamy, I must say we mustn't repeat what you said yesterday. You can't say for certain that the video we saw yesterday was related to October, 1992, and to Prozor or Travnik, and that's all the more the case in that you yourself say that what we saw yesterday does not correspond to your recollection of the events, because as you have already said, the soldiers that you saw at the time seemed to be more robust and they had these red ribbons on them whereas the soldiers we saw in the video yesterday didn't have such ribbons. So can we agree that the video we saw yesterday were not necessarily -- was not necessarily footage of the events that you observed in Prozor in 1992? I just want to be certain about this.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Necessarily, I can't say on oath that I know that footage was shot in Prozor, because I wasn't there and I didn't choose it. Your remarks about the differences, I testified to yesterday, are correct. The atmosphere of sort of looting and incineration and so on was, however, recollective of what I saw in Prozor that day. If you want to pursue this I think you have to do so with the BBC, not me, because I'm not able to help you any further. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you. I won't be contacting the BBC. The Prosecution, basing itself on your knowledge, put forward that video, showed that video. But you cannot claim that the video really relates to Prozor, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Relates to October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I can say that BBC archive included that as footage of Prozor and I took their word for it. I can't say more than that but I trust them more than I trust most media organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I think that you have failed to answer my question yet again. My question is quite simple: Are you sure or not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, neither am I going to say I'm uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to stress your attention to the list of viva voce witnesses of the Prosecutor which they filed as an annex to pre-trial brief on January 19, and, of course, the table submission of the Prosecution chart linking of 18 April. In this, you can see there are a number of paragraphs which allegedly this testimony today should be related to. And it also includes that the relevant accused is only Mr. Praljak. So I believe, Your Honour, since the Prosecution didn't ask any questions on some of those paragraphs, and I will just use two, perhaps, for example, I would like to ask the witness one or two questions related to, let's say, two paragraphs, so that after we know whether those paragraphs are having any connection with my client or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vulliamy, don't concern yourself with what we have just been discussing. These are procedural matters. But I do have to put some questions to you, questions that weren't addressed by you in the course of your testimony, so please be brief since we haven't got much time. In paragraph 7 of the amendment, it says -- indictment, it says that my client held certain positions. My question is as follows: From March, 1992, to July, 1993, do you know that my client was a high-ranking officer of the Croatian army? Are you aware of that fact or not? Please answer by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the HV, the Croatian army? I wasn't aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution ask you anything about this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether my client was the assistant minister of defence in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the course of your interview with the Prosecution, did the Prosecution put any questions to you with regard to this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in our conversations about his office in the ministry, no. Sorry any conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The transcript will be corrected. Do you know that my client, Mr. Praljak, was responsible for providing information to the Croatian authorities or, rather, to prominent people in the Croatian government, with regard to events in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period March, 1992, to July, 1993? Do you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have had such information but I don't know if I knew that particular role at the time when I -- when -- when I met him. I don't think I did know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Prosecution, this isn't discussed. Do you remember the Prosecution putting any questions to you about this matter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: About General Praljak's -- this liaison role you've just asked me about; no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I'm short of time, I won't continue. I think this provides us with sufficient information with regard to paragraph 7 and paragraph 8 in the indictment. I don't think what is stated there has anything to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just one more brief question since we were discussing Prozor and your trip to Travnik: You were there in Travnik in October, and while you were there, did you hear anything about a certain Stojak being killed? He was the head of the HVO in Travnik and, as a result, Boban visited Travnik.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Mr. Boban had visited Travnik. I didn't hear about any particular death. If I did, I don't recall it now. It's possible that it might have been in the articles, but I don't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you in fact receive any concrete information about the reasons for Boban's visit to Travnik during that period?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall concrete reasons, no. I remember not reading but having the speech - a speech he made - read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I have just one more question to put to you, and that will be it. On a number of occasions in the course of your testimony, you said that you usually went to Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Usually from Split or from the coast. Until --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after a certain date, when I was not able to visit Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you travelled through Croatia, and when you went into Bosnia, did the Croatian authorities obstruct you in any way whatsoever? Did they render your task difficult?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian or the Bosnian -- Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. On those trips, would you come across humanitarian convoys that were going to Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia? I'm talking about your stays in Croatia and then in Bosnia, but did you come across any convoys travelling from Croatia to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the roads from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia, did you ever come across convoys of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, refugees who found shelter in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I remember in Split part of the hotel we were staying in was -- had refugees, yes, and, of course, I remember some of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you about the hotels in Split. They were full and you were in Split quite frequently. Did you ever notice the refugees that had been put up by the Croatian authorities in hotels? Were they only Croats, Serbs, or Muslims, or were all these peoples represented?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority were either Croat or Muslim. There may well have been some Serbs as well but, of course, you couldn't avoid noticing them; they were everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Vulliamy. Thank you for answering my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. [In English] Your Honour, should I now put on -- I would kindly ask that all the documents I used with this -- during this cross, that they are admitted, and I could read the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's have the numbers. But before we do so, I would like to know something about the legal situation with regard to the three articles dated the 24th of October, 1993, on the firefighters in Travnik, the article dated the 26th of October concerning Mostar and Boban, and the article dated the 28th of October, 1993, regarding the events in Prozor. Are these documents that we don't have documents that the witness will provide us with as soon as possible, or are these documents that you will be tendering on your own behalf or are these documents that are of some other kind? What is the nature of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I would first like to see those documents, and then, of course, if there is valuable or relevant information, then I would submit such request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, as they say in English, you're putting these three documents on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we don't have them at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have the numbers of your documents, then, please. Mr. Registrar. Please listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be brief, the Registrar knows that the numbers start with 3D, then there are two zeroes, so I will just read out the last three numbers, if the Registry agrees. 122, 123, 124, 125, 141, 137. Your Honours, yesterday you also asked us to inform you about the source of these documents. I am in a position to do so, although I believe that everyone is now aware of the source. On the basis of the documents, document 122 is a document I found when carrying out research. It was found in the Croatian state archives. Document 123 was obtained from the Prosecution. It was an annex to the pre-trial brief. Document 124 is similarly a document I obtained, I located it in the Croatian state archives. Document 125 is likewise a document obtained from the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 68. Document 141 is also a document that I located in the Croatian state archives. And document 137 is a document obtained from the Prosecution. It was one of the Prosecution's annexes to the pre-trial brief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't want to take too much time on this issue. I do note that a couple of the documents tendered by my learned colleague Mr. Kovacic are indicated as "unofficial office translations." We, the Prosecution, would specifically reserve with respect to those documents which have not been translated by the Tribunal's CLSS. We may revisit the translations of those documents into one of the official languages of the Tribunal once we've had an opportunity to review those translations, and again, that's limited to those translations for which the translation was done by a person or persons other than the official CLSS translations, and those are clearly marked on the documents that have been proffered as "unofficial office translations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I perfectly agree with my colleague. Those documents which are presented with unofficial translation, done by my office, of course, are already submitted to the Registry department. Unfortunately, we have not yet received the translations. So as soon as we will get it, we will then consequently change the translations, because I think that the relevant is original and translation, of course, could be changed, upgraded, or any other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it seems that there are two documents for which we have official documents, 123 and 125, since they come from the OTP, and these two documents could be given definitive exhibit numbers and the others could be marked for identification. Mr. Registrar, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The following documents are therefore tendered and admitted under the reference 3D 00122, marked for identification. 3D 00123, admitted. 3D 00124, marked for identification. 3D 00125 admitted. 3D 00141, marked for identification. 3D 00137 marked for identification. Until we receive the final translation for those who are marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we have the next Defence team, please. I see two members of Defence counsel are on their feet. Normally it should be Mrs. Alaburic, unless Mr. Ibrisimovic has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have a brief, one-minute break so that Defence counsel can agree on how the time should be distributed? I'm afraid that if we don't agree on this matter, there might be some confusion. We just need a minute in the courtroom to discuss this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally it should be Mrs. Alaburic and then Mr. Jonjic, and you would be the last to take the floor, but if you would like to follow a different order, that is not a problem at all. Mr. Karnavas -- I forgot to mention the fact that Mr. Karnavas will be the last to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've agreed to try to abide by the schedule and to conclude, or rather, conduct our cross-examination as planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'd like to introduce myself. My name is Ms. Alaburic. I'm here on behalf of General Petkovic. I'm a lawyer from Zagreb. I'll put a series of questions to you that concern your work as a wartime correspondent in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The questions I'll put to you will have to do with areas that I believe to be pertinent to these proceedings. First of all, I would like to define the term of "war correspondent." Would you agree with me if I said that a war correspondent is a journalist who, to a certain extent, works as an investigative journalist because he has to carry out investigations into relevant issues, current and relevant events and relevant individuals, but such a journalist must also be very capable, he must be able to carry out a analytic form of journalism because certain statements and certain events have to be placed within a political and geographical context. So would you agree with me if I said that a war correspondent acts in the way described and combines elements of investigative and analytic journalism?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elements of those and elements of a lot of other things too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm interested in the pretext for your going to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's clarify that. You said that you went to Herzegovina for the first time in August, 1992. And you mentioned the fact that at the time, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were where -- in the area called Republika Srpska and that you reported on the centres held by Bosnian Serbs, and you mentioned Momcilo Krajisnik by name, and you said that you were told that you should be more objective -- you ought to be more objective. I see that you're nodding, or rather, that you're shaking your head. Does that mean that you didn't mention Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik in that context?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly in what context it was that you mentioned Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yes. The context was that in -- it was quite a furor that followed our entry into Omarska and Trnopolje. There was a press conference in Belgrade, and Vice-president Koljevic, as he called himself, gave a list of camps in which he said Serbs were being held on the other side. I mean, I didn't get a -- I didn't have a discussion with him. I discussed it with my editors as to how we were best to proceed, whether to, as it were, ride on the back of what we had already done in the Prijedor area, which everybody in the world seemed to be doing, or whether to take this list seriously, and as I think I put it earlier, also in purely journalistic terms, to push the agenda, to go over to the other side, and at the press conference Capljina was marked out as being apparently the worst. There was no mention of Dretelj at the time. Capljina they called it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether on that occasion any mention was made of the detention centres which the Bosnian Muslims held and in which it was the Serbs who were incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I recall was Tarcin, which was on the list. There was a tunnel under a road. When I got there -- I did go, we haven't discussed -- sorry. I -- we went there, there was nothing there. There was one that was called Konjic and, with hindsight -- which wasn't drawn attention to, and with hindsight, I wish we had gone there instead of Tarcin. I now know that place by a different name, and I wish that we had gone there instead of Tarcin, where there was nobody.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be right for me to conclude that in the summer of 1992, you did not manage to uncover a single detention centre in which there were Bosnian Muslims -- in which Bosnian Muslims held Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, yes. And as I've said, had we gone to a place I now know as being called Celebici, then called Konjic, which was not actually the one that they prioritised, with hindsight, as a journalist I wish I had, knowing now what I didn't know then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you consider yourself to be somebody who knows the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina very well in all the different entities from 1992 and 1993 as an investigative journalist when you were reporting from that area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know and saw quite a lot. I don't think anyone can claim to have seen everything, and there were whole tranches of the country which were simply out of bounds; markedly the Drina valley, we know about such things, and some of the smaller villages were simply impossible to get to, but as I think this is a rather hectic itinerary we discussed with your colleague shows one was moving around against the odds as best one could.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't doubt that. My question didn't refer to whether you knew everything. Of course, you couldn't have known everything, but do you are you consider yourself to be well-versed in the circumstances that prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the aspect of a wartime correspondent, professional criteria, the criteria of professional journalist?
