utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider myself to have tried as -- to have tried very hard to cover the war at, or the conflict or whatever we are going to call it, at as close a range as possible, which was sometimes at very close range, and very frightening. I don't like it, by the way. There is a certain kind of journalist, when you talk about war correspondents, who did nothing but war, and there were some people there. I'm not a war correspondent. I get assigned to areas of conflict from time to time but I'm not one of these people who -- and they do exist, and in fact if it is pertinent, take you up on your definition of war correspondent. I'm not one of those people who skip from war to war, as do some. I don't like them and I find them very frightening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, would you agree with the assertion that a journalist can do his job well, the job of reporting well, under wartime circumstances and events, if he spends a certain amount of time in the relevant territory, if he has the right people to talk to and relevant sources of information, and if he gets to know a social and political system, the social and political system of the country he's going to? Would that be the basic prerequisites for good journalism to your mind?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many things that you have to be able to do to do good journalism in an area of conflict. I worked very hard in the area around Prijedor with almost no contacts, as you put it, amongst the Bosnian Serb authorities that were of any use. One just simply came across them as one came across them. One was able to work there like that simply by joining a convoy of deportees. So as regards knowledge of the political situation, yes, we've discussed this political dimension, I've said I'm not a political reporter, but obviously you can't be ignorant of political developments. And what was it you said, spend time with? Sorry. I didn't remember everything you said in your question. Spend time with? Certain people. You mean in the political arena? I didn't spend very much time with political leaders during the conflict. We have talked about Mr. Boban, I've met Dr. Karadzic, and apart from in Sarajevo I don't recall meeting hardly any members of the government, SDA Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us, please, whether, according to the rules of the profession of journalist, you can fully understand statements, for example the kind that Mate Boban made, about the political system in Herceg-Bosna and its organisation, if you don't know at least something about that community and territory and its political system. So that's what I meant when I asked you about politics.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've, in response to General Praljak, admitted that I do not have, as it were, a Bosnian Croatian's -- Bosnian Croat lawyer's knowledge of the constitution, and I've admitted to that, but I do, did, and I think I still can recall, certainly did have, what could be called the layman on the ground on a fast learning curve idea of what it is that Mr. Boban was talking about and what Herceg-Bosna was intended to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] You said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are not getting the English translation of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we agree that the time a journalist spends in a certain area is one of prerequisites for knowing the situation and circumstances in that area well, and I think we will agree on that, I would like to carry on from what Mr. Peter Murphy asked you, my learned colleague, when he asked you about the amount of time you spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'd like to follow on from that and arrive at some concrete facts. Your answer to him was that it was a question of days, or rather, a matter of days was what the transcript read. Now, from that answer, may we correctly deduce that you spent not months in Herceg-Bosna but days, that it was a matter of days, as you said.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that I think was, if I recall rightly - and correct me if I'm wrong - your colleague was asking about a specific visit in August, 1992, when we went to the camp at Capljina. No. I was there in Herzegovina and in Herceg-Bosna and in Bosnia and Herzegovina for an awful lot longer than a matter of days if you're talking over a period of time. I thought that was a question about one specific visit in August, 1992. No. I was there, I don't know how many days in total but I was there for a long time during 1992 and 1993, on and off, but not just a matter of days in total, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I tried, on the basis of your testimony yesterday, to count the number of days which you specified you had spent in certain parts of Herceg-Bosna and within that framework in Herzegovina, and this is the figure I arrived at: That in Herzegovina you spent less than some 10 days in the period between August 1992 and September 1993. And when I say days, I counted every day you were there independently of the number of hours you spent there. And if to that I add several weeks in Travnik at the beginning of 1993, and other time you spent in Central Bosnia, Vitez and Travnik, it would emerge that during that period of time, you spent a total of about 30 days in the area, roughly 30 days. Of course, we cannot be precise to the day, but would that calculation of mine, based on yesterday's testimony, be roughly correct, do you think?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't done a count, but I doubt it. 10 days in Herzegovina during a year and 30 days in all? I would -- it's -- no, I can't agree with that low figure. I mean, I've been talking about specific episodes pertinent to the questions I've been asked. I was -- I was in -- you mentioned January, 1993, beginning of 1993. You said several weeks in Travnik. It was Travnik and Kiseljak. I think I talked about how we were moving between the two, and in Vitez. No. I haven't done a day count. You have. My recollection is that I've spent a lot more time than that in -- in Herzegovina and in Bosnia-Herzegovina during -- between those dates you mentioned. A lot more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You also told us that you noticed drastic differences in the situations in the different localities, between one of your visits and another; Travnik, Mostar, et cetera. Tell us, a journalist who does not spend a permanent amount of time in a given area but just comes in from time to time, is it relatively difficult for him to understand the reasons for the changes that take place and for the sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you note the changes and then you try and find out what they were. I mean, if you drive from Kiseljak to Vitez, and almost all the houses are -- or all the houses are occupied and untouched, and then another time you drive up the same road and some of them are burned out and there are signs of gunfire and shellfire, and then you drive up a third time sometime later and very few of them are inhabited or occupied, then, I mean, yes, you notice the difference, and you start to try and find out what's happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that attempts of that kind, that is to say your attempts to establish what had happened, you have to rely on information received from other people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you could give us brief answers, please, and then we will be able to get through more questions. You enumerated yesterday -- you told us yesterday all the people that you -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the main, you get your information from civilians who are still there where they were a time ago, from refugees who aren't where they were a time ago, and from the various armed forces, soldiers and official people. That's generally who you talk to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When you enumerated the people you talked to during 1992 and 1993, and I'm only referring to the Herceg-Bosna area, you mentioned today two talks with Mate Boban, Mr. Mate Boban, in August, 1992, and in October, 1992, and also the talk you had in October, 1992, with Mr. Lasic in Mostar, and on the 24th of October with Mr. Siljeg in Tomislavgrad. And then you mentioned a name on the Croatian side, Mr. Sakota, and that was in September, 1993. From your definitions of your collocutors would it be right to assume that you did not talk to anybody else who had a position either in the civilian or military structures of power and authority in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not be right. I've spent a lot of time with - I think I did mention him - Filipovic of the HVO in Travnik. I think I did mention that I was actually effectively a guest of the HVO in Travnik on one particular occasion and other occasions. I think I mentioned another senior officer, I think he might even have been the commander in Travnik, called Pokrajcic, and also, you know, one does spend a lot of time with soldiers. I mean, if we are talking about it's not Herceg-Bosna, talking about the HVO, I was with them up near a place called Tesanj, towards the north, for a long time in Tuzla with the HVO there, and one does spend time of an evening wherever one is, Tomislavgrad, Mostar, chatting to soldiers, but you said authority. But there may be others. I'll try and think. I'm sure there are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise, perhaps I wasn't precise enough as to Mr. Filipovic. Of course I didn't forget him, but my question related to your interviews, the interviews you conducted in the area of Herzegovina. Tell us now, please, when you were preparing for the interview, for an interview, for an interview with Mr. Mate Boban specifically, did you in fact prepare yourself for that interview?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first one, not in terms of the actual preparation. I hadn't -- I mean, I knew who he was and I had read about him, but I didn't do an actual sort of what one calls a library search. By the time I got to second one, October, I knew much more about him and his past and where he came from, and in a way the preparation for the interview I'd say one had done by being in Novi Travnik and Mostar during the previous few days because that's what we wanted to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, within the frameworks of your preparations for that interview, did you try and learn what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was in the first place; when it was established, why it was established, whether there were any documents on its establishment, things of that kind?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that I -- I read about it and talked about it and I know it was established before the war, and I read about the reasons, yes, as discussed with Mr. Boban, in fact, about the -- the Croatian people and their rights within Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on. But as -- as I recall, it was actually established before I met -- certainly before I met Mr. Boban, obviously, but also before the war broke out in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Tell us now, please, within the frameworks of your preparing for the interview, did you try and see what -- which municipalities made up Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did but I can't remember which of them -- I mean, I presume it was all of Herzegovina. I can't now remember how far north Herceg-Bosna went in terms of municipalities when it was established in 1991. We talked a lot about Travnik. I can't remember whether that was part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From your statement, according to which you said you were surprised when Mate Boban in the autumn or October -- in October came to Travnik and declared Travnik to be part of Herceg-Bosna, one could conclude that you really didn't know that Travnik, pursuant to a decision on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, was one of the municipalities within the frameworks of Herceg-Bosna. Or from that attitude of yours, one could conclude that you didn't have a lot of knowledge about Herceg-Bosna, the place that you were reporting about.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said I don't recall whether I knew whether Travnik was part of it, of Herceg-Bosna. What surprised me, that it was that simply it was being claimed when - and correct me if I'm wrong - it's quite an important town, strategically and historically, with a Muslim majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The substance of my remark was that you knew about the decision -- had you known about the decision to -- on the establishment [indiscernible] you would not have been surprised with the visit to Travnik or that Travnik was indeed a municipality within Herceg-Bosna, and that was in October, 1992. Now, tell us, within -- while you were preparing for your interview for Mr. Boban, and probably for the other persons that you interviewed, did you try to establish what discussions had been held on the territorial organisation and establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to that and the kind of debates and discussions that were going on and when they became topical?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one tried to follow it as best one could. This -- these -- these discussions, as you say, were being conducted on all sorts of different levels, many of them in secret. Many of them in -- in -- let's say fairly hostile political debates. I talked before about rumours of meetings between Mr. Boban and Mr. Karadzic, which he denied. There were rumours about meetings, although neither came from Bosnia, about Bosnia, between President Tudjman and President Milosevic. I mean, these negotiations one tried to keep up as best one could, and often one was being told something different by different people. So what -- I can say that we tried, yes. Back to your point about -- about Travnik, I suppose in -- perhaps I was wrong to be surprised, it's just that I referred to its Muslim majority. Perhaps most of the people in Travnik didn't see themselves as part of Herceg-Bosna. That's the point I was trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Vulliamy, that there was not a single discussion and debate on the establishment and organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina without it including territorial separation demarcation between the three constituent peoples? Do you know of a single agreement or a single set of negotiations without that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the -- there was the referendum of independence and there is the constitution, but I recognise that the constitution does include various elements that acknowledge the existence of the three, indeed and other, peoples in that country. And I'm also aware that over three years of failed peace plans also tried to take all these things into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one digression from this question to avoid any misunderstandings. When I asked you about the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, your answer was that it was established before the war. I think that it is page 95 of the transcript. Could you explain which war you meant and which year you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, of course, please correct me if I'm wrong, as I understand it, the Croatian Community, or I've also seen the term Croatian Union of Herceg-Bosna was established in 1991, by which I meant before the referendum, independence and hostilities began in Bosnia in spring, 1992, but obviously not before what we'll call the wars that began the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you speak of war and hostilities in your previous sentence, do you mean hostilities between the Croats and Muslims or hostilities in general on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talk about the beginning of the war in Bosnia? No, I would -- I would date that from the first -- well, I don't mind calling it the aggression in a courtroom, by the Bosnian Serbs, in the Drina valley and in north-western Bosnia above all, and against Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the end of 1991, the JNA, with the Bosnian Serbs, attacked a Croatian place in Herzegovina, and that that is considered the beginning of the war in Herceg-Bosna, with the Yugoslav People's Army and the Bosnian Serbs. And from this it would emerge that Herceg-Bosna was established after the beginning of the war but the war between the Serbs and Croats. Do you know about that? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became aware of it in -- during 1992. I wasn't aware of it when it happened. It was discussed, yes, by people in Herzegovina who talked about it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From your testimony yesterday, I gained the impression that you do not differentiate between the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, as a military structure of authority, as an army, from the HV [as interpreted] as the government and the civilian component of authority. Is my conclusion correct? When you speak about the HVO as a civilian military authority, from which it would emerge that we are doing a -- dealing with a unified body which is in charge of both civilian and military matters, and on the basis of that statement of yours, we could conclude that you do not distinguish between civilian and military establishment in Herceg-Bosna. Would my conclusion be correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. With respect. I certainly -- I certainly do make a distinction between the HVO and the HV. I know that one is the armed forces of -- of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the other is the army of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me. [Interpretation] I apologise but there has been a mistake in the transcript. It is page 97, line 16. I did not mention the HV, the Croatian army, but the HVO, the HVO. It's the mistake of the interpretation, so it's the HVO. We are not talking about the HV at all. It's the HVO.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Understood. Let me just reread the question, if I may. Well, when I quoted -- when I used that expression, "civilian military authority" that links the two together, I was quoting, as I recall - I don't know what his rank is - Lasic - was it Lasic? - Lasic, in Mostar. And I mean, given the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, one understands a coupling between civilian and military, but I do understand that there were -- that there were, as it were, civilian and military or entwined civilian and military columns within the HVO and in its relations to the HDZ. And I do understand that, for instance, that whereas Mate Boban was a civilian, General Praljak was a military man. I do make a distinction that they had different job descriptions, albeit perhaps a common cause.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Mate Boban had nothing to do with the HVO, would that affect your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you tell me he didn't, I would believe you because you know more about it than I do, about the structures, but judging from the meetings with him and the language that he used during those meetings, and the -- and the people who were in his headquarters, particularly the second and third ones in Grude, and the way that he talked about the HVO, one would be given to believe that he was very close to it and would regard himself as having influence if not authority, as a civilian, influence in -- over its movements albeit, as you rightly say, formally not direct command over it because he's not a military man, but he spoke about the -- the HVO as though he was not entirely distant from it. I would add that when we waited for him to -- for his meeting to break up in the cellar before our second conversation, well, all of his company were military men and most of them were in the HVO, if not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will now conclude our discussion on this topic by saying that you really are not well familiar with either civilian or military structure. Now I would like to put a question to you pertaining to Mate Granic and what you stated on page 81, line 12 and 13, of yesterday's transcript; namely, that Mate Granic, Croatian foreign minister, in July of 1993, stated that Croatia was prepared to help with the mass deportation of 50.000 people and that in that context a meeting was held in Makarska in order to implement this deportation. Did I interpret your yesterday's evidence correctly? I was trying to quote it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did. I wasn't at that meeting. I was told about it by people who had, from the United Nations High Commission on Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In his book, "Foreign Affairs, Behind the Scenes of Politics," described this meeting, Mr. Granic, and among other things, said that that meeting was attended by the government representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the BH army representatives, headed by Vice-president Hadzo Efendic. Then he continued on to say that several BH government ministers attended the meeting as well, including Hasan Muratovic and Kasim Trnka. I don't think there is any reason to distrust Mr. Mate Granic when he writes about this in this book. He was himself present at the meeting. Therefore I would like to ask you whether you truly believe that those attending the meeting in early July of 1993 truly discussed that issue, namely how to deport 50.000 people from Bosnia-Herzegovina or were they perhaps trying to find a solution to this very important issue?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported what they told me. They didn't tell me the names that you've just mentioned. They told me they had been at the meeting, that was the bit of the agenda they discussed, and the bit of the agenda that I testified to yesterday, having been told what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Also in relation to Mr. Mate Granic, yesterday you said something recorded on page 102 of the transcript, namely that in September of 1993, Mr. Sakota, before the visit of the Red Cross -- so Mr. Sakota told you that before the visits of the Red Cross, Mr. Granic had called, telling him to improve the conditions at the detention centre. Could you please clarify the meaning of what you said. Did you say this in the context implying that Mr. Granic was aware of detention centres but was only trying to improve conditions there and keep them at this improved level, or were you trying to say something different?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Granic was or wasn't aware of, but I take it he must have been aware of the existence of these places to have made the call at all. I was reporting what Mr. Sakota told me, that he had received this phone call and had been asked to, I think it was some -- I don't recall the exact quote, it's something to the effect of make these people's lives a bit easier. But I can't tell you what Mr. Granic did or didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not asking you that. I'm not asking you about what Mr. Granic knew. I'm just trying to establish what meaning you ascribed to that, and thus I'm asking you this: Are you familiar with all the activities conducted by Mr. Granic starting from July, 1993, onwards, aimed at terminating, disbanding detention centres and, in the meantime at least, improving conditions therein?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know specifically about disbanding detention centres but I knew from newspaper reports that he was, if I recall rightly, and -- that he was not regarded as necessarily one of those in Zagreb who particularly agreed with some of the things that were going on. That he was active in negotiations and so on. But I didn't -- I wasn't aware of any particular demands by him with regard to camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have several more minutes left before 3.00 and I'd like to use that time. When you were telling us about your conversation with Mr. Mate Boban, you said that almost identical positions on cantons were contained in Vance-Owen Plan, and that the HVO, in a jocular way, referred to that plan as "Thank you, Vance-Owen." Are you familiar with the plans of the international community about the territorial structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the plans that existed before July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were various plans. I mean, forgive me, madam, there were so many plans that after the event, they -- I remember the headline in Oslobodjenje: "Clinton Trazi Novi Plan." Another one. Yes. There were the those that arose I think out of the London summit of August, 1992, I think even various attempts before then, but certainly I was aware that Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance, when they were appointed, were not the first, but you'll have to forgive me. If I have to go through them all, the Carrington, Cyrus Vance, Owen, Washington, Geneva, I'm not sure that I can recall the details of each and every one. I remember an extraordinary arrangement of maps and various ideas, but at the time I was following them very carefully and I would not guarantee that I can remember the details of each one now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That was precisely the thrust of my previous question. Did you know that there was a single conversation where the borders and maps were not discussed? Borders and maps within Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now I'd like to turn to this: Do you know of any country where there are several peoples residing there, peoples who have the status of constituent nations without that country having a complex structure in the sense that it's a federation, confederation, it's a country with cantons; simply speaking, a country with a complex internal structure?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can think of countries with complex internal structures that were not born of violence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about violence. I'm putting a principled question to you and I think it will be quite important for us to see how you interpreted the statements of Mate Boban and the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So do you know of a single country which would not have a complex structure and which would have two or more constituent peoples residing there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I stick with my first answer. This discourse was happening in an atmosphere of violence, and I thought at the time it entailed violence, and it did. But yes, I do, and he knew -- he knows them too. Switzerland is one of them, Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Switzerland is a complex country, as far as I'm aware. It has six cantons, so I don't think that that's a proper example for my question.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only mentioned it because he did and because it has people who speak three languages and I actually didn't know how many cantons Switzerland had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since yesterday, and today, when asked by General Praljak today, you said that you were a bit tired of the use of the word "narod" meaning people. I have to ask you this, and this will be quite useful in order to properly evaluate your answers provided both yesterday and today: Do you know that in order to protect the rights of a people -- do you know of any other way of protecting the rights of a people without guaranteeing them a constitutive status? In other words, in your view, when founding a state exclusively on the basis of rights of citizens as individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are putting the same question as that put by Mr. Praljak, and the Prosecution objected to that question. Please go ahead, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again for the record, Mr. President, we object. This has gone way beyond the realm of this witness's testimony and this is now into the level of a complex political discussion, which really has little or no relevance to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to conclude very soon, because we have to take a break, but prior to that I have to repeat to Defence counsel, you are putting political questions and, yes, you are allowed to do that. However, bear in mind that here, at this Tribunal, political context is mentioned in each judgement, sometimes in the annex of the judgement, but at any rate it doesn't take more than two or three pages. The Judges have to evaluate criminal responsibility in a particular factual context, and all the time that you use up for such questions - and you can use up as much time as you want - is not going to be properly reflected in the judgement because the Judges will not evaluate this, and thus I have to intervene in view of the rules on cross-examination pursuant to Rule 90. You have to bear in mind that you have to phrase your questions in such a way as to elicit answers which will have legal value for your clients. We are not here to investigate history; no. We are here to decide on criminal responsibility. It's 3.00 ten minutes now. We will make a 20-minute break, but before we do that, let me remind you that the Prosecutor had four hours to examine this witness. Based on our calculations so far, and I will ask that our legal officer confirm this, based on our calculations you have already used up 162 minutes and you have 78 minutes left and there are three more Defence teams, including yourself. Or rather, three plus yourself. We will resume at 3.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We have another hour and a half left. Mrs. Alaburic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded with my portion of the cross-examination, and out of respect to the Chamber, my colleagues and Mr. Vulliamy, I would like to say this, in view of my last question: It wasn't my intention to elicit any kind of a political remark from the witness. However, it's been 14 years since this witness talked to Mate Boban and yet he was still able to quote his words as to why he was unable to accept the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and why he believed cantonal structure to be appropriate for Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the witness very emotionally - at least, that's how I read it - told us that he was very tired of how the word "narod" was used in the former Yugoslavia. Therefore, based on that, I thought it important to put this question to distinguish between a civic state and a state which has nations as constituent elements because I believe that views on that affect somebody's way of reporting. As for the reports and their style, I believe that they had some political side to them, which is normal. And that's what I wanted to say by way of explanation and it seems to me that the witness would like to say something as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked -- may I, Your Honour? Because at the beginning of that, you did ask a question about, as it were, there wasn't a political question, it was about my interpretation of the word "narod," and I'm grateful for that because, you know, when I said I was wary of the word, I'm not casting aspersions on anybody's identity, culture, history, language. What I meant was I was wary of its use and deployment in the former Yugoslavia by then. I was wary with what people were doing with it. And throughout 1991, and I know this is elsewhere, I'd listened to people tell me that wherever there were the "Srpski narod" was Serbia. I'd heard it in Knin and in Eastern Slavonia, which are both in Croatia, and I saw what the deployment of that word had done. It's not the word that I was wary of, nor do I mean any offence to a people's identity or history or culture or whatever. What I was wary of was the way in which that word was being used by people to precede acts of violence, and that was in particular during the second conversation with Mr. Boban when he said that the Croatian "narod" was armed and ready to defend its freedom, in the light of what I had experienced in terms of the use of that word, I was wary of the way in which it was being used, not -- by way of casting aspersions on any culture or identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you kindly for your explanations. That's precisely how I interpreted your words and this is why I wanted to direct your attention the word "narod" as a constituent element in the theory of a creation of a state. But I think that we've devoted enough time to this issue. I want to thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vulliamy, my name is Tomislav Jonjic. I will be putting questions to you on behalf of Mr. Valentin Coric. These questions will cover some of the topics mentioned previously by my colleagues but I'll try to explore some other angles and some other details which I believe to be important. Today, when asked by Mr. President and then later on when asked by some other colleagues, you said that you did not deal exclusively with analytical journalism but also combined it with investigative journalism and that that entailed quite complex and detailed preparations. Can you please tell us, the first time when you came to Bosnia-Herzegovina, what did you know then about Bosnia and Herzegovina? How did you prepare yourself? What did you read and who briefed you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought -- I think I have at least begun to answer your question already. I did not have -- I'm not an expert on the Balkans. I had what I would call an informed layman's view of the history of Yugoslavia. I had read books on the history of Yugoslavia during the Croatian war of independence in 1991. By the time I got to Bosnia-Herzegovina, I had what I'll call a layman's knowledge. As I say, my work was not -- I wasn't a commentator or a columnist; there were plenty of people doing that who were experts on Balkan history. I was assigned there as a journalist, but when you say "investigative," it usually means something else. It means exposing corruption, or long-term investigations. It wasn't necessarily my job to analyse politically as a Balkan expert the situation, but it was, I agree and accept entirely, my job to understand it as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You mentioned that you used the transportation of the British Battalion of UNPROFOR, in view of the existing roads in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did I understand you well that the members of British Battalion transported you several times from one location to the next one?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not many times, no. I accompanied them in my own car on a number of occasions, including one in which we were quite seriously and frighteningly ambushed by the Serbs, but I didn't use their vehicles very much at all, no. If I gave that impression before, it was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did the commanders or officers of the British Battalion give you some instructions or information about what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, yes, in two different ways. One was informal, and I wouldn't say off the record but it was informal and that was when we would be based in Vitez, where they were also based, and sometimes we would eat in their canteen, if there was nowhere else to do so. And then the second level, they gave fairly -- towards -- I mean after a while, they gave formal press briefings, with maps on developments, front line movements and, of course, their own activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You, as a British journalist, undoubtedly are well aware of the fact that in a part of the British press and also in the publishing industry and also historiography, there are some unfavourable opinions about the history of the British Battalion and generally about the role that Britain played in the wars in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to think that -- I can't speak for the whole British press. I'd like to think that where there were -- credit where it was due, criticism where it was due, but for the most part straight reporting. I'm not aware of any unnecessary -- didactic hostility apart from perhaps extreme left-wing publications that I don't take so seriously which were talking about imperialism and stuff. That didn't interest me. I'm not quite clear on what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I don't think there is any need to go into greater detail regarding that. I would just like to ask you several things to try to establish how well you were aware of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If I understood you well, on page 20 of today's transcript -- yes, page 20, of today's transcript, lines 15 through 18, you mentioned that it was only during your last visit to Mostar, which was in February of 1994, that you, to your great surprise, realised that the BH army controlled several blocks of buildings on the western bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my first visit I wasn't aware that they had territory on the other side, that's correct. On the west side. I learned that actually in between my two visits, and during my February visit wanted to have a look at the state of things on the western side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And that is when you realised that the ABiH also had some territory in the western side of the river under its control?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In between my visits in September and February, I learned that from other reports, but I didn't know that in September when I first went, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement given in 1997, and also in the testimony that you gave yesterday, you said that you once met Mate Boban when he was celebrating the fact that Stjepan Kljujic had been replaced, or rather, he had been appointed the head of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna authorities. You said that Kljujic was moderate and he was replaced by Mate Boban who was not moderate. Have I understood that part of your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I used the words "moderate" or "not moderate" as succinctly as that but the gist is correct. I had a long conversation subsequently with Mr. Kljujic about that episode. He called it a putsch. His word, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I'd now like to show you a document that comes under 65 ter, P -- D 00049. That's the document. Have a look at the first column on the left and have a look at the first part of the second column. It's an article from a publication called Croatian Monitor, dated the 24th of May, 1992. It's called a historical agreement between Croats and Muslims. For the sake of the transcript I would like to point out that it is an opposition publication, not a governmental publication, in the Republic of Croatia, and as you can see -- as a journalist you're probably used to reading through articles very quickly. You can see that they mention historical meeting that was held in Split on the 17th and 18th of May, 1992. You can see that it was a meeting of the HDZ from Bosnia-Herzegovina and of the SDA. The HDZ from Bosnia-Herzegovina was represented by the then representative, Mr. Miljenko Brkic. On that occasion, an agreement was reached, and at the bottom of the page, if we can see it, have a look at the part that has been underlined. You can see that both sides reached an agreement on a confederal relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. As a result, the agreement reached in Graz had been revoked, the agreement between the Croats and the Serbs, and in the last line, it says all the parties in Croatia were unanimous in greeting, in accepting this new Croatian-Muslim agreement which was approved by Alija Izetbegovic. You can find this at the top of the second column. It follows that Stjepan Kljujic wasn't immediately replaced by Mate Boban, which is the impression one gains on the basis of your testimony. However, what is more important is that I'd like to know that when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina in August, 1992, at that time were you aware of the fact that there were such agreements between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I don't recall whether I knew about this specific meeting, but indeed I did know that there were agreements between the Croats and the Muslims. And interestingly, that's the first confirmation I've heard about the -- seen about the former agreement between Mate Boban and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: If you read through this carefully, you'll see that it's not referring to an agreement but to a meeting in Graz, not an agreement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm at the wrong bit of the page. There was something about the revocation of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You've got the right page but it's right up at the top. Or in fact we are looking at the top. If we can just have a look at the bottom. Can you scroll down, please. Have a look at the part that has been underlined. It's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the word "annul."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: It starts with the words "With this meeting ..." and you can also see the words "the recent meeting" appearing in that part. It says "the recent meeting" not "the recent agreement," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand corrected, it does say"meeting." I'm not quite sure how you annul a meeting, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's something that we'll establish in the course of the proceedings. Thank you very much. Now with the help of the usher I would like to show you another document. It's a 65 ter document. 5D 00064 is the number of the document in question. This is a matter you're probably more familiar with since it's a report on the agreement between President Tudjman and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic. And they have agreed in a similar manner one month earlier and the HDZ from BH and the Party of Democratic Action reached an agreement. In item 5 it also says that the Republic of Croatia supports the efforts of the international community in its attempts to put an end to the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to put an end to military action. Were you familiar with this document at the time, or if you weren't familiar with the document itself, were you familiar with the attempt to reach an agreement on the part of the Muslims and the Croats in the mid-1990 -- in mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm correct, it's one month later, not earlier, unless I'm mistaken. I don't recall whether I was aware of this particular declaration and meeting. I suspect I had read about the meeting. I'm not familiar with this particular document, but I was certainly aware that at that time - and I think we are talking about May in your previous document and June here - there was an intention to be in alliance or at least a relationship of friendship politically, and I think I've testified to how I saw that alliance work militarily on the ground at first, and indeed continued throughout the war in some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that context, and not even two months later on, in August, 1992, you visited Mate Boban in Grude and you spoke to him. General Praljak put a question to you about that event. But since I have a quote in front of me, I'd like to be a little more precise when putting my question to you. Yesterday, on page 28 of the transcript, lines 1 to 5, you said that Mate Boban said, and I quote you, "that he wanted the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into cantons on the model of Switzerland." In response to Mr. Praljak's question, page 45 and 46 of the transcript, you said you didn't know much about Switzerland. I was fortunate enough to spend a few years living in Switzerland so I probably know a little more than you do about that country and I do know that Switzerland consists of cantons but is a unified country. Can you explain why Switzerland has unified cantons whereas the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when based on this cantonal model, is equivalent to the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already pleaded relative ignorance of how Switzerland works. I don't know whether the cantons are ethnic, I honestly don't know whether you have a French, German and Italian canton in Switzerland. I didn't get from that meeting with Mr. Boban that he was -- any sense that he was aspiring to -- he didn't talk much about the unification of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If anything his remarks were tended towards the opposite direction. He was saying he could not respect the constitution for reasons we've been discussing at length. He said that he could not accept Sarajevo as the capital. So I can't talk about Switzerland as regards how its cantons are organised, but yes, it is a unified country. All I can say is that from Mr. Boban's remarks, I didn't get the impression that he was wanting to emphasise the union or unification of the country which had been internationally recognised and proclaimed independence from Yugoslavia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He didn't use that term, and if he did, he didn't use it enthusiastically. I also, by the way, don't know whether Switzerland groups its cantons either ethnically or in terms of other names. I don't know if there is an equivalent to Herceg-Bosna in Switzerland, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I hope we'll clarify this with one more question. You didn't use a neutral word. You didn't say -- you didn't use the word the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina when you assessed the way Mate Boban spoke about cantons. You used a very charged word, you referred to the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is why I'm putting this question to you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fair question. By "division," I was, I think, inferring a separation of sorts along ethnic lines and, from what I gathered, these were intended to be as exclusive as possible ethnic lines in these cantons. I mean, one of the things I noticed in support of my answer was that as the conflict developed that we are concerned with now, Herceg-Bosna manufactured its own car number plates, for instance, its own postage stamps. I remember the time when the land lines started to work at last in Central Bosnia, at the PTT stations, but the area code was 385, which is the area code of Croatia, and I remember you could call Croatia but you couldn't call, say, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We'll look into that later on but with regard to the stamps, the money, et cetera, are the notes used in London and Edinburgh, are the bank notes used in those two cities identical? Naturally we are referring to the same state.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fair point. They are not identical, as you know. There is a Bank of Scotland and a Bank of England.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to another series of questions that have to do with HOS. For the sake of the transcript I would like to point out that we'll probably agree that the abbreviation HOS stands for the Croatian Defence Forces. H stands for Croatia, and naturally the HOS is to be distinguished from the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council. I don't know whether this distinction is clear enough in the English language but I believe it is. For you, however, the distinction to be made is crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Forces" certainly has a more military connotation to me than "council," which perhaps pertains to the previous -- your colleague's cross-examination over this civilian-military entwinement. But thank you. That's precisely my point. The HVO was, so far as I could see, or did involve an entwinement, whereas the HOS, I'm not quite sure what their actual status was but I knew that they were affiliated to a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. We'll come to that later. First I would like to ask you the following: When you first appeared in Bosnia-Herzegovina in August, 1992, what was the relationship between the HOS and the HVO? Were they on friendly terms or was there any form of antagonism between these two groups?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've testified that one of the things that I went to look at was a report that one of the leaders of the HOS, if not the leader, whose name I can't recall at the moment, I think it's Kraljevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Kriminaljevic"], had been, as the HOS put it, executed at a roadblock, and I didn't talk a great deal to Mr. Boban about the HOS, although I think we might have done a bit, but did talk to Mr. Dedakovic, of the HOS in Capljina, a great deal about the HVO, and it was a long discussion about territorial aspirations, which I think I've testified to already, or reported what he said, and also very importantly for him, went back to disagreements over the defence of Vukovar which as you know is something of a sacred scar in Croatian history.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would like to show you document 5D 01013. I'd like to show you this document again. The English translation has been attached to this document, as we have an English translation attached to all the other documents that will be shown. We still don't have the document. Yes, that's the document. We can see it on the monitors now. We have the English translation in front of us. This is from the command of the HOS war HQ for Herzegovina. It comes from -- it's dated the first half of August, 1992, because in the second line it says because the deputy commander of HOS was arrested on the 7th of August, 1992, and then continues to say that the HVO and other forces attached to the HVO were self-proclaimed forces whereas HOS was a regular military force in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It says that all members of the HVO shall be arrested, in the second paragraph. The HVO is accused of being an instrument of the KOS, counter-intelligence service, and UDBA, the state security administration, and the greeting is -- at the end is, "We are ready to act for the homeland." Mr. Vulliamy, yesterday you said that in Capljina you saw photographs of Ante Pavelic. You saw the letter U - it's on page 32 of the transcript - and you also spoke to Dobroslav Paraga, the president of the Croatian Party of Rights in Zagreb. That is page 36 of the transcript, lines 12 to 14. You would agree that when one has a look at the document, the relationship between the HVO and HOS was not ideal and HOS was considered to be an integral part of the regular armed forces, the so-called regular armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, can I just say that my attempt to recall the HOS leader's name has been transcribed as Kriminaljevic, which may or may not be a joke but perhaps that -- to answer your question, I -- sorry about that. The -- I was under no illusions at all that the HOS and the HVO were in an antagonistic relationship. I didn't know that HOS regarded itself as a legitimate armed force and that the -- thought the HVO was an illegitimate armed force. That seems to be between them. So far as I was aware the HVO was actually the official armed force of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, not the HOS, so I'm -- I'm learning this as I go along. As regards your reference to Ante Pavelic and the Ustasha, I inferred, I think rightly, that the HOS regarded themselves as, as it were, the descendants of the movement. In fact, their use of the term "za dom spremni" sort of indicates that, and although I did see Pavelic's picture in Grude, and the capped U, I don't think I ever tried -- if I have -- no, I don't think -- I didn't see anything in HVO literature that claimed the descent of the Ustasha movement. However, during my time there, HOS soldiers did visibly come under HVO command during 1993, because we got to know their roadblocks and the same people changed -- at least on one occasion in particular, changed uniforms but, of course, I understand that at the beginning the relations were very antagonistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about the year 1992. We agree that the HOS referred to the Ustasha movement and to the Independent State of Croatia, and I said it had descended from that movement. I won't go into history, but in the course of the Second World War, this movement was on the side of the Third Reich. You yourself have confirmed this. You yourself have agreed that the HOS was in fact the military faction of a political party, the Croatian Party of Rights. With your leave and with the usher's help, I would like to show you document P D 00093. We have the English translation on the screen. It's an order from the president of the Croatian Party of Rights, Dobroslav Paraga, an order in which certain HOS officers are being appointed or promoted in the municipality of Maglaj, which is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you know.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've been there, and it was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And this supports what we have already discussed, the claim that HOS functioned under the auspices of the Croatian Party of Rights. While you were in Herzegovina, did you know anything about the ethnic composition of HOS units?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were Croats, Bosnian Croats and Croats, indeed, and Bosnian Muslims were also in the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of the ratio between the Croats and Muslims in HOS units?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I imagine it varied from region to region. I think quite apart from the whole question of the divisibility or indivisibility of Bosnia, it probably accorded -- at least, in my experience, it accorded to whether there was a Bosnian army presence in the area or not. And I think around Capljina, at least, there might have been but it was -- I think HOS was probably a better bet if you wanted to get a gun to fight the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: With the usher's help I'd like to show you another document now. It is 5, number 5D 01012. And it is an excerpt from a book, I don't know whether you know the book, but it is by Mehmed Dizdar, and it is called, "Fated Stolac." It has 260 pages and it would be a considerable feat for the Defence to translate all of it. We have chosen certain fragments -- or rather "Stolac on Trial," written by Mehmed Dizdar. We have extracted a few pages for the purposes of this cross-examination, and we also attach the English translation. The author of the book, Mehmed Dizdar, until the beginning of the war, was one of the commanders in the police station of Stolac, and later on he was one of the key figures, key organisers, of the BH army in the Stolac and Capljina areas. May we look at the first page of the translation, please. Page number 1. That's it. The author of the book describes a dialogue which took place in the summer of 1992 with one of the commanders of HOS, and then if you look at the second half of this translation, the author asks a question: Who else is in HOS? And the person he's speaking to Beso, he was a Bosnian Muslim by name and surname, he says, all the Muslims in HOS, all of them are in -- all of them are Muslims. How do you get along with the HVO, it should be. There is a mistranslation here. It should read, How do you get along with the HVO, not the HOS. We have our line, nothing to do with them, is the answer. Tell me now, please, Mr. Vulliamy, do you find it strange that the vast majority of HOS members in Herzegovina belonged to the Muslim ethnic group, were ethnic Muslims, at least according to what Mr. Dizdar says in this book of his?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of the book or of him, I'm afraid. If this is true, it -- I -- I suppose -- I don't know what to say. Perhaps it confirms my view that it varied from region to region. The HOS people I got to know up near Prozor on their roadblock were all Croats, and I think Mr. Dedakovic was half Serbian so -- but I don't know of this book. I don't know of its veracity, nor do I have any reason not to think it true but I think I've said that I knew that there were Muslims in the HOS and the further away from --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll come back to that book or to details from the book, which have to do with the events in Herzegovina. A moment ago we mentioned the letter dated the 7th or 8th of August, 1992, in which the HOS commander in Mostar is called the regular army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would now like to show another document, 5D 00130. It is an order dated the 15th of August, 1992, signed by Sefer Halilovic. I'm sure the name rings a bell. Sefer Halilovic at that point in time was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as you can see, he was issuing this -- he issued this order that the HOS units from Konjic, Jablanica and Prozor, under the command of Major Zvonko Lukic -- I don't know if you're well-versed, or rather, are you familiar -- can you judge on the basis of a name which ethnic group this Mr. Lukic belongs to or could be, ethnically speaking, but let me tell you that quite certainly he's not a Muslim, on the basis of his name.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can hazard a guess. He's probably a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: He could be either a Serb or a Croat, I don't know, but at any rate, the HOS units in those three municipalities under his command are being subordinated to the command of TG 1 in Konjic. From this, may we deduce that the command of the BH army was in command of the HOS units?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, they were able to issue an order to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you yourself said that the political goal, or rather, the territorial goal of the Croatian Party of Rights and HOS was to include the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the Croatian state, can you explain to us in what way that would have been acceptable to the Muslim leadership and Sefer Halilovic and Alija Izetbegovic? Was that not diametrically opposed to what they advocated in public?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that either Halilovic or Izetbegovic anticipated Bosnia being incorporated into one large Croatia, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you there. Yes. But the question is what was HOS's role with the -- that -- those kind of territorial and political goals within the frameworks of the armed forces of BH?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, I -- I -- I -- in my experience, HOS people that I knew went under HVO command. Clearly in this instance they go under the command of the Bosnian army. I'm not privy to the -- to when or how the HOS broke up, if they ever did, or to whom they allied. They seemed to be going off in all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you that because yesterday you described to us your first visit to Dretelj, when HOS was in command, and that was the summer of 1992, when you, on page 34 and 35 of yesterday's transcript, stated that at the entrance to that detention centre, there was a soldier wearing BH army -- a BH army uniform. We can therefore conclude that in 1992 the Dretelj detention centre was commanded, administered, both by Croats and Muslims within HOS together. However, for us to clarify the role of HOS, with your permission, and I'm trying to save time, of course, because it's running out, I would like to ask the usher once again to go back to Mehmet Dizdar's book, that is to say document 5D 01012. And it is the translation of pages 164, or part of that page. We don't have it on the screen yet. We need a translation of page 164, please. That's the next page. That's it. We are dealing with the same time period, the same speakers, and while the author of the book is asking what HOS's plans are and what they intend to do, this other man, Beso, who was a highly positioned officer in HOS says, "We are all going to join the army, that's to say the BH army. As soon as the conditions are in place. Such is the mood within the army, and the Muslims in the HVO have the same opinion." So already in the summer of 1992, the Muslims in HOS and the Muslims in the HVO are in fact preparing to join up with the BH army, to move to the BH army. If we look at the next page, it is a dialogue that took place in August 1992. The author of the book, as one of the organisers of the BH army in the Stolac and Capljina area, is talking to Avdo Hebib. I don't know whether the name Avdo Hebib is familiar to you. He was one of the top politicians in the Party of Democratic Action for ten years and he was deputy foreign minister. I don't know if you've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You haven't. Fine. In that conversation, and we are not going to read it all out in view of the time, but they are discussing the BH army organisation in Stolac and Capljina, and then Hebib says to the other man, he's describing how they tricked the Serbs, and we saved ourselves and the HVO was allegedly engaged in terror, and Hebib says, "We'll trick them too." He was consoling him, and he meant the HVO, the Croats. Tell me, please, from the excerpts we have just read, are we able to conclude that the Muslims in the HVO and in HOS, already in 1992, if this testimony is correct, planned operations against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to tell with these extracts from a book I haven't read and people I haven't heard of or the veracity of all this. It seems they want to trick them. It seems there are Muslims in the HVO, which indeed there were. I think I've testified already about how many of those were arrested on the front lines and taken to Dretelj when we went there. I'm not quite sure what the question is. But if I'm supposed to understand that gist of what Mr. Boban was saying in the meeting that we are talking about, that all this was an extension of the HVO's problems with HOS, he certainly didn't go into it with me. I can talk about what was said at that meeting. It's difficult for me to talk about this book, but it doesn't sound as though whoever is saying this, planning operations may be, I don't see that, but it's quite clear and I think we've made the point -- I've -- I'm not disagreeing with that you that relations between the HOS and HVO in 1992 were not good, were bad, hostile. I've said that. But during the conversation with Mr. Boban, it was the relationship with the constitution and this was -- he wasn't preoccupied with HOS despite the fact that one of the things we wanted him to talk about was the -- the killing of this man on the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jonjic, it is 4.25. I'm getting a little worried because the Pusic and Prlic Defence counsel are probably going to take some time, or are they going to give up their right to cross-examine? I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have reached an agreement. I don't think there will be any difficulty. I need just three or four more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask Mr. Vulliamy to clarify a detail that cropped up today when you were questioned by Mr. Praljak and when HOS was mentioned in the context of the fall of Jajce. In view of the fact that at that time, and we are talking about the end of October, 1992, you were in Central Bosnia at the time, do you know that there was a joint command set up at the time, of the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Jajce?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? All over the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia. Where we had Colonel Blaskic, Anto Prkacin on the Croatian side and so on, but if you know nothing about that, just say so.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew there was a -- there were movements towards a joint command. Whether it went into effect or any length of time or not, I don't know, but I certainly remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And two more short questions. On several occasions during your testimony yesterday, and you repeated that today, that in order to send out your reports and articles to London, you had to go to Split, Imotski, that there were no links from Tomislavgrad, et cetera. Am I right in understanding that you had to cross into Croatia in order to send your reports out? Did you have to cross the border?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varied with the different -- in the different periods. Some people had satellite phones. I didn't. We had access to those. The phone I mentioned in Tomislavgrad was somebody's satellite phone that we were able to use once. I don't remember if there were land lines in Tomislavgrad at the beginning of the war, I don't think there were. Split and Imotski were certainly the places where you could depend on getting one, in Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Telephone lines were down quite certainly from Herceg-Bosna. And now my last question: Yesterday, on pages 80 to 82 of the transcript, you said that the imam, the religious leader in Capljina, the imam, and numerous civilians over there and representatives of the UNHCR told you that for the Prosecution of Muslims and from Capljina and Stolac, that the most responsible person was Mr. Pero Markovic, that they considered him to be the most responsible person. And you mentioned that on pages 36 and 37 in response to a question from Mr. Murphy, but only in relation to Capljina. And you mentioned the information you received from the UNHCR. I'd like to clarify this matter. Did this information refer to Capljina and Stolac and Dretelj, by the same token, and were -- was the information given by the UNHCR, was it confirmed and borne out by the imam and other civilians that you managed to talk to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't return to speak to the imam or the civilians in Capljina after talking to the UNHCR. I'm afraid I can't answer your question with regard to Stolac. It was the name that came up during conversations with the imam and the women in Capljina and I think I've described the conversation with the UNHCR about this man and their view of his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes my cross-examination, Mr. President. I should like to tender the documents that were shown the witness into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, you have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The following documents are admitted into evidence: [In English] therefore tendered into evidence, 5D 00049, 5D 00064, 5D 01013, 5D 01012, and 5D 00130. I hope that I haven't left any aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, so we now -- we would now have 30 minutes left. You have a document you've forgotten?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President, but it seems to me that the document with the final digits 93 has not been included in that list of documents. It's the order of the 4th of September, 1992, Dobroslav Paraga; 5D 00093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This exhibit is therefore tendered and admitted under the reference 5D 00093. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So theoretically speaking, we have 30 minutes left for questions by Mr. Pusic's Defence counsel and Mr. Prlic's Defence counsel, and perhaps any supplementary questions and questions from the Judges. I'm an optimist. Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: My name is Roger Sahota, I'm the co-counsel for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I couldn't see you, you were right behind the pillar there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: My name is Roger Sahota, I'm the co-counsel for Mr. Pusic. On behalf of Mr. Pusic, I'd like to ask you a few questions. You've given evidence in some detail about your visit to Dretelj in September, 1993, and you've also given evidence about the press conference [Realtime transcript read in error "president"] that took place some days later in Medjugorje, also in September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Could I ask for a correction in the translation? The word "president" should read "press conference." I think when you gave evidence you implied in your testimony that the first time that you came across my client, Mr. Pusic, was at this press conference; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it was, yeah, and the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: You also gave evidence to the effect that before your visit to Dretelj, you had spent some time trying to obtain access to that detention facility.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried the previous day before General Praljak gave us permission, and had tried once in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And you had no success until you came across General Praljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I don't think it's in dispute but it was General Praljak who gave you permission to visit Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes, as I hope I've described accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: When you were trying to obtain permission to visit Dretelj, did anyone suggest to you that you should contact Mr. Pusic, that he was somebody in authority who might be able to obtain access for you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: During your visit to Dretelj was Mr. Pusic's name ever mentioned to you by anybody or in particular by the commander who was your escort, Commander Sakota?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Could you just clarify this: Did anyone ever mention Mr. Pusic's name to you prior to September, 1993? Had you ever heard his name mentioned in any context?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I knew his name, and I think, to the best of my recollection, the first time I heard it was the first day I saw him, which was at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to the press conference, you gave evidence earlier today that the meeting, the conference that you went to was chaired by an individual called Kresimir Zubak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said chaired by, I think he made the opening remarks and appeared to be the driving force of the panel, but I don't know. I don't know if he chaired it. He introduced or chaired it or some such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Is it correct that you hadn't met Mr. Zubak before but you had heard of him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard of him but I had not met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And Mr. Zubak announced himself as the holder of a certain office. Could you tell us what that office was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he called himself the vice-president of the HVO, but I wasn't sure quite what that meant or whether that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you also have told this Court that you don't speak B/C/S fluently; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've had this conversation. I spoke it very basically a while back and I don't -- I've remembered very little of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I know that the press conference took place a long time ago but can I ask you to see if you can remember whether there was an interpreter on the panel of speakers that day.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was said must have been interpreted. I can't remember whether the interpreter was on the panel. I presume yes, because a lot of the people there were -- I'd say about half were from the international press, but I'm afraid I can't recall where the translations came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that you just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I mean, there are two ways of doing this: Sometimes there is an official translator, sometimes it's your own translator doing it. I can't recall which was that on that occasion but what was said was obviously translated because I was taking a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: But the speeches were certainly given in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Final question: Is it correct to say that you had never come across Mr. Pusic before and you had never heard his name mentioned in any context prior to that press conference?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, that's as I recall, no, and I mean no and yes: No, I hadn't heard his name, nor had I met him until the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy, I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Counsel Sahota. There is a good example of cross-examination well conducted, which I'm sure will inspire Counsel Karnavas. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours, and thank you for the confidence you bestow upon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vulliamy, I just have a few questions. I wanted to pick up where you just left off a little bit ago with respect to Mr. Zubak. As I understand it, you indicated that you heard his name subsequent to this press conference as well and you tracked his career thereafter to some degree.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
