utterances.text: I wouldn't say followed it, but he did hold political office, if I remember rightly, in the Federation at some point, and it's a name that recurred, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it that as you sit here today you don't recall whether he was the one that replaced Mate Boban when Boban stepped down.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said the Federation, maybe that's what I meant but I think my uncertainty demonstrates that I knew he held some kind of office but I wasn't quite sure which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the title of your book, "Season in Hell" also says "Understanding Bosnia's War." That's kind of an ambitious title, the subtitle, "Understanding Bosnia's War," wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it ambitious? I don't know. Yes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I say that because the Bosnian war was rather complex.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some ways yes, in some ways no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Give you an example: You had indicated earlier that you were somewhat surprised to find Muslim HVO soldiers now being detained in a prison and you made a comment about that, I believe yesterday. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean not necessarily surprised given what had been going on by then, but I think I testified as to sort of, you know, what I call the spirit of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is, has its inimitable collegiality, and I remember feeling and discussing with colleagues if not surprise, certainly a sort of -- a disheartened feeling that comrades could arrest their own comrades who had been in combat together, it -- quite possibly for at least a year, against the Serbs to the east of where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Then you would have been equally surprised, I take it, to learn that on June 30th, 1993, HVO Muslim soldiers killed HVO Croat soldiers in their sleep in Bijelo Polje and in the North Camp. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, and I find it similarly disheartening for the same reasons I've just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so if you have a certain element within your own ranks that are killing other members, you would find it understandable why some of them at least would be put in prison or why there might be some distrust; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the episode you're talking about, but I -- certainly that does not sound like what I called the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Collegiality.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the collegiality of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, getting back to the issue of HOS, my colleague Mr. Jonjic was kind enough to share with us a couple of documents, and I just want to touch on that a little bit. You were obviously aware, if not then by today you are, that HOS was part of the ABiH, the army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I knew that there were Muslims in HOS, yes. I'm not sure that I was aware that there was a direct chain of command. Nor -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll buy that, okay?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say nor was I aware that orders could be given from Sarajevo to the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe it was General Praljak who indicated that it was Alija Izetbegovic who had promoted a certain person to the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember his name, but I remember General Praljak asking me, and I hope I said no, but because I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was the gentleman that was killed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Jonjic shared with us the ambitions of HOS, which were to push the Croatian borders all the way to the Drina, which would have meant taking up the entire BiH, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I've testified to that after my conversation with Mr. Dedakovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to paraphrase you, or -- I don't want to put words in your mouth, but you seem rather surprised, or it seems oxymoronic that here you have Alija Izetbegovic in bed with HOS whose ambitions are to push the borders all the way to the Drina. It seems a little ridiculous, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you seem to paraphrase me. "In bed with," I'm not in a position to say that. "Ridiculous" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't find it odd?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me odd that the -- that a Bosnian party would advocate complete incorporation into a Greater Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Unless of course, we look at the other documents that were shared with us by Mr. Jonjic which shows that the Muslims that were in HOS and again in HVO had ulterior motives; that is, at some point to trick the Croats, take the weapons, and move over to the ABiH. That's another way of looking at it, wouldn't it, which would make sense then.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the veracity of this book, and I don't -- I mean, I can't -- I mean, it could be that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that scenario would make sense then, wouldn't it, why Alija Izetbegovic would support HOS with their territorial ambitions, if he had Muslim fighters with the intentions of at some point taking their weapons and switching sides?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read into his head or what was going on. This is all -- this was all behind the scenes. It sounds to me like there was some manipulation going on, which wouldn't surprise me, in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly, and there was a lot of that going on in the war, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to hit just some high points because I don't have a lot of time. With regard to Herceg-Bosna, you indicated that you thought it was well organised. You mentioned the currency, Mr. Jonjic pointed out in Scotland they use a different currency than perhaps there in England. Do you know whether the central bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina was actually functioning at the time? Were you aware whether it was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that it started functioning at some point, but I don't know when. With regards to the Scottish thing, it's -- I mean, the country code for Scotland is 44 and you can call Edinburgh from London.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just work --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it sounds irrelevant, but you're making it relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Work with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down for the sake of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Work with me on the central bank, okay? Do you know for a fact - yes or no - was the central bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioning at the time as it should?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when it should have been functioning, and I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please slow down a little since the interpreters are having a little trouble following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was Sarajevo under siege at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know when it was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, my question now is: Was Sarajevo under siege? That's my question. I'm sure you understood it. Please answer that: Yes or no, during that period.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And was the Sarajevo government, the state government, was it able to function as it normally would have during peace times?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't mean to be aggressive. I'm just trying to move along. Sorry, I don't want you to think I'm trying to be offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Just bear in mind, then, the interpreters need some time to interpret what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, and I do apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now a little bit about your background. And I don't want to go into too much, but basically, as far as I know, from listening to you, you are a foreign correspondent and covering this particular war off and on, and your covering snippets of it, or selective portions of it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you say, off and on, on and off, I was visiting, but over a substantial period of time. The fact that I wasn't there all the time was a matter of editorial decisions but also a matter of stamina. I can only think of one or two people who were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm not being critical, so don't -- Now, I take it from listening to you, you hadn't -- you didn't read -- well, first of all, you're not a trained lawyer. You're not a trained lawyer.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a trained lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or a constitutional expert.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a constitutional expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't have the opportunity to look at the constitution of the former Yugoslavia or of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read books about the history of Yugoslavia that would have made references to both but I certainly can't say I ever read the full document of either, no, I didn't, and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that you didn't look at the legal framework and the legislation that was put in in establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about its establishment but I didn't read the legal material, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you had read the establishment, obviously you would have learned that Travnik, at least, when HVO -- I mean HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formed back in, I believe it was November 18, 1991, it was at that time that Travnik came in to that community.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've answered that question. I wasn't clear. I think your colleague asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to stay on that particular point, because I -- yesterday, when I heard you - and correct me if I'm wrong - I was under the impression that you wanted to give the -- you drew a conclusion that after meeting Boban, and after reading that Boban had gone to Travnik and declared it as part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the day after or shortly thereafter the conflict broke out and you were trying to connect these two together, these two events or three events together.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I was trying to connect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you connected them.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the events happened in rapid succession. I can't remember if -- I would have to go back to the transcript to work out exactly what I said. Yes, there were comments that it was all happening very soon after his visit. I don't think I ever said he went to Travnik to declare war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But you nonetheless place a certain amount of premium on him going to Travnik and then shortly thereafter the war or the conflict broke out as a result of, as you had indicated, Boban declaring that Travnik was within the fold of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I'd have to go back to the transcript to look at exactly what I said, but certainly after that happened, things happened -- the violence erupted pretty quickly. Or at least the ultimatum that led to the violence started, things happened very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But as a reasonable person you don't exclude the possibility that one had nothing to do with the other?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exclude it but there was conversation about the coincidence for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now were you aware that on October 17th, there was a presidential meeting of the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, there in Travnik? Were you aware of that and that might be the reason why Boban was there, not for any other nefarious reasons?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read about that meeting on the 17th, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware that on October 21 in Novi Travnik, the commander of the HVO in Travnik, Stojak, S-t-o-j-a-k, was killed? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you mention it, I think I was and, of course, I was with the HVO hiding behind a wall during a firefight on, I think, the following day, or at least two days after that, and that's probably where I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason -- why I'm talking about Travnik, Novi Travnik, Prozor, those areas are all nearby each other, they are not that far apart?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prozor is quite a long ride from -- but the first two are close to each other, yes, and tarmac connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated Prozor, you translated it into as "window," was rather important. If it would be important for one side, it would also be important to the other, right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So whoever controlled that area, you know, would control -- you know, would be -- would have the upper hand?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall - again, I'd have to check the transcript - I used the word "gateway," Prozor was strategically important to -- militarily to anyone who wanted power in west -- in Central Bosnia and was also important in terms of the distribution of aid. I was asked earlier about aid convoys to Croatia. As you know, by the time they got into Bosnia it was quite another matter and I had to cover a story of one that was actually stopped and ransacked by the HVO at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In that area I believe there is a chapter you title "land grab" or something to that effect. You talk about an individual by the name of Mahmut Alagic [phoen] who talked about the Muslim triangle. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that conversation, yes, and I do recall writing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that particular individual was describing to you the Muslim strategy for what areas they wanted in that particular region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's what he was saying, exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Getting back to this whole thing with "narod." I know we only have a few minutes left but I just wanted to touch a couple of things on that. One of the basic issues, at least what you hear and what you read in the press, was that at the time there is this notion of a unitary system; one person, one vote. That was one of the main sticking blocks or issues with the Croatians in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure we talked about one man -- one person, sorry, one vote, but I do recall Mate Boban talking about his preoccupation that the constitution guaranteed the rights of individuals but not of "narod."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not of "narod," right. And this thing of "narod," which is translated "peoples" or "nation," is a little bit different than nationality, would you agree with me on that, without going into too many details?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is neither of those three; it's "narod."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To translate it into German is didactic, but that's the nearest I can get, if we can obliterate the obvious use of the word "das volk" during this last century.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, okay. But nonetheless at no time, from reading your statement, reading your book, do you say that Mate Boban indicated that he wanted that part of Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna to become part of -- geographically part of Croatia; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've testified to this many times: He never used the word "annex" or "secession," but when he talked about the fact that it wasn't part of Croatia he lamented it and talked about unfortunate historical circumstances and other ways in which, if you like, the Bosnian Croats, for want of a better word, or term, were, as I think he said. He said this over and over again, culturally, spiritually, et cetera, affiliated to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sort of like the Greeks and the Cyprian Greeks. Just as an example that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps the Ulster Protestants in Great Britain, which I always thought was a better example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, just a couple more points. When you got over there in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I take it you were aware that Croatia had been attacked by the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, when I got to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you first got there --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You obviously must have been aware that Croatia was attacked by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was more than aware of it. I had spent an awful long time covering it in Vukovar, Osijek. I was very aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you must have been aware also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please slow down. Because we have problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Obviously then you must have been aware that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was used by the JNA as a staging ground in attacking Croatia.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly aware that the JNA was based in Croatia -- sorry, in Bosnia, particularly in the north, and reported quite extensively on that, across the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That was a time when Alija Izetbegovic was the president of the Presidency, right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rotating Presidency, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It never rotated, trust me.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He took power and held it for eight years.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do u recall what his response was when Ravno was attacked on May 5, 1991? Is it -- November, September? In September, 1991. I'm sorry, I got the wrong date. I thought it was autumn.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Ravno had, with hindsight, not the -- not the attention it deserved. I don't recall the reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well the reaction was, This is not our war. Of course the citizens of Ravno were Croats and not Muslim but they were in BiH. Now, thinking back, how do you think that might have made the Croatian peoples, "narod," of Bosnia-Herzegovina feel when the president of the Presidency says, after a village is wiped out, says, it's not our war?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not here to apologise for the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. There are a few more points I want to make, but we are out of time, and I want to thank you very, very much for coming here, and have safe travels back home.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. You used the exact amount of time allocated to you, and I'm grateful for that. It is good when everyone follows the guidelines as far as time is concerned. Mr. Mundis you have no additional questions to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no further questions for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will discipline themselves too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a single question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have had extensive conversation with Mate Boban. You gave us the impression that he had presented himself as the leader of the Croats of -- of Herceg-Bosna, as if he were God, more or less, politically. Did he ever in any way hint that there were other Croats and that there might be an authority -- another Croat authority beside him to which perhaps he owed respect or even a certain obedience?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to understand and to explain but also certainly pleaded my ignorance on the exact relationship between him and the HVO and the armed forces. I don't know whether he was in a position, as in the leader of a state in our democracies, to order the armed forces to war, but he certainly spoke as though his intentions were intended to be carried out, and I think -- I referred to some line in which he said, "No one will go to Geneva except on my authorisation." There was another thing about any one who disagrees should depart or leave in some other manner. He talked as if his word was not quite as deified as God but he talked as though he ran the show, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to put a brief question to the witness. Witness, I'd just like you to clarify something with regard to the testimony you gave this morning and with regard to Mr. Pusic. In response to Mr. Sahota's clear and precise cross-examination, you confirmed that you saw Mr. Pusic for the first time at the press conference in Medjugorje. And that he didn't seem to be in a position to influence the decisions taken. Could you be a little more precise with regard to his lack of influence, bearing in mind the fact that you said this morning that Mr. Pusic was responsible for prison exchanges. So did he have any influence with regard to the detention conditions in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I apologise. I can't really enlighten you on what influence he did or didn't have. He introduced himself or was introduced as -- I can't even remember the expression, but in charge of prisoner exchange. I don't know what influence he did or didn't have. But he did seek to not justify the conditions in Dretelj but he did seek to persuade the conference that they fell within the requirements of international law of war. Also, this matter of prisoner exchange, I mean, one of the things I remember we discussed was that it didn't seem as though the inmates of Dretelj were there for exchange. I went to quite a few places that were basically collections of pawns in a chess game where -- who were just interned for exchange, and they invariably on all three sides knew that that's what they were there for. I don't think anyone in Dretelj said that they were there for exchange, and indeed, the fact that some of them had been there several, several weeks suggests, although not conclusively, that they weren't. So I can't really help you, I'm sorry, with regard to the influence that Mr. Pusic did or didn't have over that except to make that observation, that they didn't seem to be, for want of a better word, what I'll call an exchange detention centre. Some of them had been there since July so it seemed that they were more permanently interned. Sorry, I can't help you more on his influence. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Vulliamy, this concludes your testimony. On behalf of all the Judges, I would like to thank you for having testified over this two-day period and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to Mr. Mundis with regard to the testimony of the expert witness that will be held tomorrow. My first question is whether the expert witness is available for the Chamber, and my second question is how much time do you think you will need for your examination-in-chief? And how many documents do you intend to show him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the first two questions, I think I'm in a position to answer those. The third question, I'm afraid I'm not going to be of much assistance. Dr. Donia is here, Dr. Donia will in fact be ready and available to testify commencing at 9.00 tomorrow morning. My understanding from my colleague Mr. Scott, who will actually be leading Dr. Donia's evidence, is that we anticipate that direct examination to take approximately two hours. I am not in a position at this point to indicate the number of documents that Mr. Scott will be intending to show the witness. I can perhaps seek to get that answer as quickly as possible for the benefit of the Chamber and the Defence, but I believe we will certainly take him through his report and a number of the documents that he cites to in that report. Mr. President, my case manager indicates that there are approximately 35 documents that we have here that will be shown to the witness, but again, I'm hesitant to say much more than that simply because, again, Mr. Scott will be leading the witness's testimony and he obviously is not in the courtroom at this moment, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this gives us an idea. It will take up -- your examination will -- in chief will take about two hours, and we have about 35 or 40 documents that will be shown to the witness. I'm now turning to the Defence teams. We will be commencing tomorrow. We'll start at nine and conclude at five, and then we will have another hearing on Thursday morning which will end at 1.45, so you have to bear this schedule in mind when planning your cross-examination. If you fail to reach an agreement by tomorrow, we will then apply the rule of a sixth of the time allocated to Defence counsel, but I believe that you will be able to reach an agreement. However, tomorrow, it's Mr. Kovacic who should start the cross-examination, because everyone is taking this in turn. So you should meet, reach an agreement, and tomorrow at the beginning of the hearing you will tell me how you have decided to divide the time. I should also point out that on Thursday, at 1345, everything will come to a halt. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, since you indicated that I would be the first one on question, and based on the discussion we already have -- we already had on how to deal with Expert Witness Donia, I presume that -- all of us together, we presume that providing we agree on how to go with that witness, that we will also have, how shall I say, a right to suggest that another counsel will lead that witness, and most probably -- I guess I can inform you that in advance, most probably or highly probably, one counsel, and this will be my colleague Mr. Karnavas, will take all the time we can get. However, but I don't think this is now time to discuss this second issue which I'm raising, it is a matter of time because even -- but, if you allow me, I will discuss that now, but probably the best time will be after the direct, because then we will -- all will be aware of how the issue is complicated or perhaps not complicated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ideal solution would be for you to discipline yourselves and for you to inform us of who will be cross-examining the witness and when. Unfortunately, we have to bear in mind time restrictions. We have no choice. I personally would like to have far more time to deal with all these matters, but unfortunately, time is limited, and as a result, it's necessary for you to reach an agreement. If you fail to reach agreement, in that case we will apply elementary mathematical rule that we have decided on you will take it in turn to cross-examine the witness. If Mr. Karnavas will be starting tomorrow, well, he'll be starting tomorrow, but the only thing that counts for us is that on Thursday at 1.45 it is -- it will be necessary to have concluded with the hearing of this expert witness. Reach an agreement, discuss the matter, and try to decide on the important questions you want to put to the witness. If we are dealing with expert matters, it's not necessary to ask the same question ten times. It's a very serious affair. You're all very experienced, and what is important is to provide the Judges with the necessary information. That is the purpose of this exercise. If we fail to meet this objective, we will have wasted a lot of time and you will have wasted a lot of time for your Defence. It's ten past five. I apologise to the interpreters because we have worked a little longer than usual and we'll have the pleasure of seeing each other again tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
